label: Reference aid; the AHJ and the printed NEC govern.

sections.title: Article 600 — Electric Signs and Outline Lighting
sections.plain_explanation:
This article covers signs, outline lighting, and skeleton tubing — the lighted advertising and identification equipment on commercial buildings. Its field core is simple: a proper sign branch circuit and a real disconnect at the sign.
The numbers that size a sign job:
• Sign branch circuit — 20A minimum, serving signs and outline lighting only (600.5)
• Pedestrian entrances — at least one outlet in an accessible location at each entrance to each tenant space of a commercial building or occupancy accessible to pedestrians, for sign or outline-lighting use, supplied by a branch circuit rated at least 20A that supplies no other load (600.5(A)); service hallways and corridors are not considered accessible to pedestrians
• Load calculations — each required sign branch circuit is figured at not less than 1,200 VA in feeder and service calculations (220.14(F))
• Neon and skeleton tubing — the high-voltage secondary wiring follows its own part of this article (600.31 and 600.32), and the tubing and its power supplies are listed equipment, not field-fabricated parts
• Circuit ratings — 600.5(B): circuits supplying signs with incandescent and fluorescent sources are rated 20A maximum; neon transformer or power-supply circuits are rated 30A maximum
• Disconnect — each sign needs a disconnect per 600.6
sections.on_the_job: If a bid has signage, price the circuit and the disconnect, not just the sign. On a strip-center tenant build-out, that means the dedicated 20A sign circuit back to the panel, the outlet at the tenant entrance, and the disconnect at the sign itself per 600.6 — and 1,200 VA carried in the service calculation for the required circuit, whether the letters' nameplate adds up to that or not.
sections.figure_idea: Storefront with a channel-letter sign fed from its own labeled circuit.
sections.why_it_exists: A sign is serviced by sign techs, not electricians, often years after the install, on a ladder, on a building face. The dedicated circuit keeps sign faults and sign work off the building's other loads, and the disconnect at the sign gives the tech a real way to kill the letters before opening them. The entrance outlet exists so the sign circuit is planned at rough-in, not borrowed later.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is figuring the sign circuit at the connected load of the letters — a few hundred volt-amperes of LED — and moving on. For feeder and service calculations, 220.14(F) floors each required sign branch circuit at 1,200 VA. Undersize the calculation and the service is wrong before the sign is even hung.
inspection_fails: Sign fed from a general lighting circuit shared with other loads.
No disconnecting means at the sign (600.6).
Sign circuit figured at connected load instead of the 1,200 VA minimum in the service calculation.
Required outlet missing at a tenant entrance accessible to pedestrians.
Neon secondary parts field-fabricated instead of listed tubing and power supplies.

sections.title: Sign branch circuits — 20A, signs only
sections.plain_explanation:
600.5 puts a dedicated circuit behind every storefront sign, in two parts:
• 600.5(A) requires at least one receptacle outlet in an accessible location at EACH ENTRANCE of each commercial building or occupancy that is accessible to pedestrians, supplied by a branch circuit rated at least 20A that serves no other load. That outlet is there for the sign and outline lighting at that entrance.
• The sign circuit itself is the same family of rule: a sign or outline lighting system is supplied by a branch circuit rated at least 20A that serves no other loads, other than signs and outline lighting tied to the same work.
• Service hallways and corridors are not considered accessible to pedestrians, and delivery doors are not pedestrian entrances — the entrance-outlet rule does not reach them.
• In feeder and service load calculations, each required sign branch circuit is figured at not less than 1,200 VA.
sections.on_the_job: Don't hang storefront lighting or receptacles on the sign circuit. On a strip-center storefront in Kissimmee with two pedestrian entrances, the layout is: one receptacle outlet at each entrance, and the sign on its own 20A home run back to the new Siemens panel, breaker labeled SIGN, with nothing else on it — not the display lighting, not the window receptacles. The service calculation carries that circuit at 1,200 VA. Sharma's S-01 already sets a 20A minimum on commercial branch circuits, so the code and company practice land in the same place here.
sections.sharma_note: S-01 already sets a 20A minimum on commercial branch circuits — the code and company practice land in the same place here.
sections.figure_idea: Storefront sign on its own labeled 20A circuit.

nec2023_change.change: The sign circuit can now also feed equipment that controls the sign, and the delivery-door and service-corridor exemption became a formal exception. The dedicated sign circuit can now also carry loads that control the sign, such as a time clock or photocell (Exception No. 2).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 600.5 Sign branch circuits

sections.why_it_exists: The sign is the one load every storefront has to run, service, and relamp — often by a sign contractor who is not the tenant's electrician. A dedicated 20A circuit means the sign never shares with whatever gets plugged in beside it, and the entrance outlet means the sign crew is not running cords through a doorway or tapping a circuit that was never meant for them.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is tapping the sign circuit for the storefront display lighting because the sign circuit is right there and 'only half loaded.' Under the 2020 rule the 20A circuit serves signs and outline lighting only. Feeding the sign's own control gear — a time clock or photocell — off that circuit is a 2023 change, not the 2020 rule.
inspection_fails: Storefront or display lighting tapped off the sign circuit.
No receptacle outlet at a pedestrian entrance of a commercial occupancy.
Sign circuit rated under 20A, or shared with another tenant's loads.
Sign circuit figured below 1,200 VA in the service load calculation.

sections.title: Sign disconnecting means
sections.plain_explanation:
Every circuit that feeds a sign, an outline lighting system, or skeleton tubing gets a real disconnect — not just a breaker back at the panel.
• The control is an externally operable switch or circuit breaker that opens all ungrounded conductors at the same time.
• Location: at the point where the circuit enters the sign enclosure, the sign body, or the pole the sign is mounted on.
• The 2020 rules in 600.6(A) also cover the within-sight, lockable, and remote-location marking situations: a disconnect that is not within sight of the sign must be capable of being locked in the open position, and a disconnect in a remote location must be marked at the sign, so service people and first responders can find and kill it.
sections.on_the_job: Pylon sign at a Winter Garden shopping center: the sign circuit comes out of the tenant panel on a dedicated 20 A Siemens breaker (the sign circuit family in 600.5), runs up the pole, and lands first on an externally operable disconnect mounted at the point where the circuit enters the sign structure — one switch opening all ungrounded conductors. The sign tech kills it, locks it, and opens the cabinet with nobody able to re-energize from the panel. On a monument sign whose disconnect ends up remote, inside the building, the sign itself gets a placard telling the tech where that disconnect lives.
sections.figure_idea: Sign disconnect at the point of entry into the sign body, placard for a remote disconnect beside it.
sections.why_it_exists: Sign work happens on ladders, on rooftops, and inside metal cabinets full of ballasts, drivers, and high-voltage neon secondaries. The person servicing the sign has to know the circuit is dead — and stay sure of it while both hands are in the cabinet. A disconnect at the point of entry, opening every ungrounded conductor, is the one control that does that; the lockable and marking rules keep it true when the disconnect has to live somewhere else.
inspection_fails: No disconnect at the sign — when the inspector asked, the crew pointed at the panel breaker.
Disconnect opens only one ungrounded conductor; the second hot stays live inside the cabinet.
Disconnect mounted remotely with no marking at the sign telling anyone where it is.
Disconnect not within sight of the sign and not capable of being locked in the open position.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'the breaker in the panel is the disconnect.' A panel breaker is overcurrent protection and a control, but 600.6 puts the disconnecting means at the point where the circuit enters the sign enclosure, body, or pole — and if it is not within sight, it must be lockable in the open position and marked. Naming the panel breaker leaves the sign tech with no local, lockable kill point.

sections.title: Retrofit kits (new in 2020)
sections.plain_explanation:
Converting an existing sign to new lighting technology is a listed-kit job, not a lamp swap.
• A general-use or sign-specific retrofit kit must be listed and labeled, and it must include installation instructions for field conversion of the host sign.
• The kit is installed per those instructions.
• Wiring methods follow Chapter 3, with the Class 2 path in 600.12(C), 600.24 and 600.33.
• Parts that are not replaced are inspected, and damaged parts are repaired or replaced.
• Workmanship follows 110.12.
• The retrofitted sign is marked per 600.4(B) — including the alert label where tubular LED lamps run on the existing sign sockets, so nobody later installs fluorescent lamps.
The 600.2 retrofit definitions — host sign, subassembly, and general-use and sign-specific kits — ride with this section.
sections.on_the_job: A shopping plaza on Orange Blossom Trail is converting its cabinet signs to LED. Before quoting, the estimator confirms the kit is listed for that host sign and plans the 600.4(B) label as part of the job — an inspector can fail an unlisted conversion even if it lights. On the first sign the crew finds two heat-damaged lampholders; because the kit job includes inspecting the parts that stay, those sockets are replaced before the LED tubes go in, not after a callback.
sections.figure_idea: Host sign opened for conversion: listed kit, instructions, and the retrofit marking label.

nec2023_change.change: Section 600.35 had redundant requirements removed, which are already covered in Chapters 1-4 of NEC.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 600.35 Retrofit Kits

sections.why_it_exists: A lamp swap leaves the old sign's ballasts, sockets and wiring in service with lamps they were never listed for. Heat, mismatched drivers and tired lampholders are how sign fires start. The listed kit, its instructions and the marking tie the converted sign to a tested combination — and the alert label stops the next technician from screwing fluorescent tubes into a sign that has been rewired for LED.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating the job as a lamp swap: pull the fluorescent tubes, drop in LED tubes, done. If the kit is not listed for the host sign, or the sign is not marked per 600.4(B), the conversion fails even though it lights — and where tubular LEDs run on the old sockets without the alert label, the next lamp change can put fluorescent tubes back into a rewired sign.
inspection_fails: Sign converted with an unlisted retrofit kit — 600.35 requires a listed, labeled kit with installation instructions.
Retrofitted sign not marked per 600.4(B); no alert label where tubular LED lamps use the existing sign sockets.
Heat-damaged lampholder left in service during a retrofit — parts not replaced must be inspected, and damaged parts repaired or replaced.
Kit installed contrary to its instructions, with the old ballast left connected where the kit requires it removed.

sections.title: Article 604 — Manufactured Wiring Systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Manufactured wiring systems are factory-built wiring assemblies — plug-together branch-circuit and feeder components — used heavily in office fit-outs. The system is field-installed, but the assemblies cannot be inspected at the site without destroying them, so the listing does the inspecting: components must be listed and used as one system, never mixed between manufacturers (604.1, 604.6).
• Permitted in accessible, dry locations, and in ducts, plenums, and other air-handling spaces where listed for it and installed per 300.22 (604.4)
• Cables are listed Type AC or Type MC, or listed flexible metal conduit, with 600-volt copper conductors from 8 AWG to 12 AWG and a full-size copper equipment grounding conductor (604.6(A))
• One exception: a luminaire tap not over 6 ft long, feeding a single luminaire, may drop to conductors as small as 18 AWG (604.6(A) Exception)
• Support follows the Chapter 3 article for the cable or conduit type used (604.6(E))
Where Sharma meets it: relocatable wiring for office partitions, pre-wired workstation feeds, and raised-access-floor whips on tenant fit-outs. The connectors are keyed to the system — a whip that will not mate is the system telling you the parts came from different manufacturers, and forcing the connection voids the listing. Home runs land in the panel like any other branch circuit; the manufactured part is only the distribution between the connection point and the outlets, and every run stays accessible so it can be inspected and reconfigured without disturbing the building wiring.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma hits these on tenant work: an Orlando office fit-out with 40 workstations fed from raised-floor whips on two 20 A branch circuits. Keep one manufacturer's system end to end and follow its instructions — the home runs are field-wired to the panel, and everything past the connection point is the listed system. Get the furniture vendor's power plan into the job file before rough-in: it shows where each feed lands, and finding out at trim that the whips are another maker's costs a day, not an hour.
sections.why_it_exists: A factory assembly arrives with its splices and terminations already made, and nobody on site can open it up and check them without destroying it. The listing, the keyed connectors, and the one-manufacturer rule stand in for that missing inspection: they keep a 277-volt lighting whip from being plugged into a 120-volt system and keep untested field splices out of a ceiling plenum.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer treats a manufactured wiring system like ordinary cable: mixing one maker's whips with another maker's distribution boxes because the plugs almost fit, or assuming any AC or MC cable qualifies. The system is listed as a system — the cables are listed Type AC or MC with 600-volt, 8 to 12 AWG copper conductors, and parts are not interchangeable between manufacturers.

sections.title: Article 605 — Office Furnishings
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 605 covers the electrical equipment, lighting accessories, and wiring systems used with office furnishings — cubicle panels, partitions, workstations, desks, shelving, and storage units that interconnect mechanically and electrically to form one system (605.2). A lone motorized desk on its own cord is not a system, and is not covered.
• Powered furnishings connect to the building wiring at the fixed connection point the system is listed for — never by a cord pushed through a wall or ceiling.
• Partitions interconnect only with the manufacturer's listed connectors, or a flexible assembly identified for the use, in the combinations and circuit counts the listing allows. Where flexible cord makes an interconnection, it must be extra-hard usage, 12 AWG or larger, with an insulated equipment grounding conductor, not over 2 ft long, joining mechanically contiguous partitions (605.5).
• Fixed partitions — secured to building surfaces — are permanently connected by Chapter 3 wiring methods; freestanding partitions may be hard-wired the same way (605.7, 605.8).
• A freestanding group may instead be fed by a single cord and plug when every 605.9 condition is met — see the checklist table.
• Lighting accessories must be listed for use with the partitions and supported; they carry no receptacles, and a cord-connected light uses hard-usage cord not over 9 ft (605.6).
• Wired partitions are not permitted to extend from floor to ceiling unless the AHJ specifically permits it.
sections.on_the_job: Office fit-out in Lake Mary: Sharma's scope is the building side. Two dedicated 20 A circuits on Siemens breakers feed receptacles set within 12 in. of where the furniture plan lands the powered partitions — roughed in before the furniture truck arrives, not after. The furniture vendor's shop drawings are an electrical document on this job: they show where each building feed lands and how many circuits the system is listed for, and they belong in the job file before rough-in. Coordinate furniture power early; the furniture system is listed equipment, not field-built wiring.
sections.why_it_exists: Cubicle systems put receptacles and lighting inside fabric-covered furniture that office staff rearrange with hand tools. The listing, the listed connectors, and the hard caps on cords and receptacle counts keep a furniture layout from becoming unlisted field wiring hidden inside a partition — and keep an overloaded furniture circuit from cooking unseen.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating the furniture feed as a convenience problem: "plug the cubicles into the nearest receptacle on a shared circuit." A cord-connected group needs its own dedicated circuit, a receptacle within 12 in. of the partition, one cord not over 2 ft — and never more than 13 receptacles in the group. Second trap: running a multiwire circuit inside a cord-connected group. Not permitted at all.

sections.title: Article 610 — Cranes and Hoists
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 610 covers the wiring, disconnects and controls for cranes, monorail hoists, hoists and all runways (610.1). Rare in Sharma's current work — recognize it, and price from the article when a warehouse job includes one.
• Runway disconnect (610.31): the contact conductors along the runway get their own disconnect between them and the power supply — readily accessible and operable from the ground or floor level, lockable in the open position (110.25), opening all ungrounded conductors at once, and within view of the runway contact conductors.
• Crane disconnect (610.32): every crane and monorail hoist carries a second disconnect in the leads from the runway conductors, also lockable open. Its rating is a 610 rule, not a 430 rule: at least 50 percent of the combined short-time ampere rating of the motors, and at least 75 percent of the sum for any single motion (610.33).
• Sizing follows the article's duty-based approach (610.14(E)), not a straight Article 430 feeder calculation: largest motion at 100 percent of nameplate, next largest at 50 percent, and a Table 610.14(E) demand factor when several cranes share one conductor system.
• Contact conductors are located or guarded so nobody touches energized parts by accident (610.21(A)). Festoon and pendant wiring is supported so strain never lands on the terminations — a traveling crane beats on its wiring every cycle.
sections.on_the_job: On a warehouse bid, find the crane's disconnect and runway-conductor scope in the drawings before pricing. Worked case: a bridge crane with a 30 A hoist motor and a 12 A bridge motor — the 610.14(E) conductor load is 30 A plus half of 12 A, 36 A, not an Article 430 build-up. If the crane package is by others, say so in the bid notes — otherwise the runway disconnect and the lockout point land on Sharma by default.

sections.why_it_exists: A crane runway can stay energized along a whole building, out of reach, while people work under moving loads. The mechanic on the bridge and the rigger below both need the conductors dead when the job says dead. The two lockable disconnects — runway and crane — make a real lockout possible, and guarded contact conductors keep hands and tools off live parts the rest of the time.
inspection_fails: No disconnecting means for the runway conductors, or one that cannot be locked in the open position (610.31).
Runway disconnect mounted where it cannot be operated from the ground or floor level (610.31).
Crane or monorail hoist with no disconnect in the leads from the runway conductors (610.32).
Contact conductors where a person can touch them inadvertently — not located or guarded (610.21(A)).
Festoon cable supported by its own conductors, strain on the terminations.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing the crane feeder like an Article 430 motor feeder — biggest motor at 125 percent plus the rest at full rating. Article 610 runs on duty: largest motion at 100 percent, next at 50 percent, demand factor for shared runways (610.14(E)). The 430 answer oversizes the run and misses the question.

Not less than the 610.14(E) and (F) calculation

sections.title: Article 620 — Elevators, Dumbwaiters, Escalators, Moving Walks, Platform Lifts, and Stairway Chairlifts
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 620 covers the electrical installation for elevators, dumbwaiters, escalators, moving walks, platform lifts, and stairway chairlifts. Sharma's scope is the electrical side; the machine itself belongs to the elevator contractor under ASME A17.1.
• Each driving machine gets its own disconnecting means — an enclosed, externally operable fused switch or circuit breaker — and it must be lockable in the open position only, never lockable closed (620.51).
• The disconnect kills the driving machine only. Car lighting, receptacle, and ventilation circuits (620.22, 620.23, 620.24) are arranged to stay energized, so service work in the car is not done in the dark.
• GFCI protection: every 125-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-ampere receptacle in pits, hoistways, on cars, and in wellways and machinery spaces is GFCI type, and machine-room receptacles carry GFCI protection too (620.6).
• Where several machines share one feeder, the disconnect overcurrent devices are selectively coordinated with the supply-side devices, selected and documented by a licensed professional engineer or other qualified person (620.62, 620.65).
sections.on_the_job: On a Central Florida medical-office job with two hydraulic elevators, Sharma's piece is the two machine-room disconnects, the car light and receptacle circuits tapped ahead of them, the pit GFCI receptacles, and the machine-room circuits — the elevator contractor sets the machines and traveling cables. Confirm that split in the bid, not on site: where one feeder serves both machines, the coordination selection and its documentation are a line item too, not a free extra. One disconnect per machine, lockable open only, and the car circuits stay live when it is off.
sections.figure_idea: Machine room: one labeled disconnect per unit, car circuits tapped ahead of it.

nec2023_change.change: Received substantiation specifies which cable types may be installed in elevator raceway or traveling cable. Shielded pair cables, coaxial cables, and communication cables complying with 800.179 are now specifically permitted in Section 620.36. 620.51(A) Type. Ex. No.

sections.why_it_exists: A mechanic working in a hoistway with a machine that can still move, or in a car gone dark because the disconnect killed the lights too, is how people get hurt on elevator work. These rules split machine power from the service circuits: the machine can be locked out dead while the car stays lit, and the receptacles a mechanic plugs into are GFCI protected.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating the elevator disconnect like an ordinary motor disconnect and feeding the car lights through it. It feels tidy and it is wrong twice: the disconnect must not kill the 620.22, 620.23, and 620.24 car circuits, and it must be lockable in the open position only. A disconnect that can be locked closed fails even if everything else on the job is right.

rows: Stays energized — not through the machine disconnect (620.22–620.24)

inspection_fails: Car lighting fed through the machine disconnect — disconnect off, car dark (620.51, 620.22).
Disconnect lockable in the closed position — 620.51 permits lockable open only.
Plain receptacle in the pit — 125V pit receptacles must be GFCI type (620.6).
Two machines on one feeder with no selective-coordination documentation (620.62).

page_quiz.explain_plain: 620.51 requires the disconnect to be lockable in the open position only — it is not permitted to be lockable closed.

page_quiz.explain_plain: The disconnect must not disconnect the car lighting, receptacle, and ventilation circuits of 620.22, 620.23, and 620.24 — they stay energized for service work.

page_quiz.explain_plain: 620.6 requires GFCI-type receptacles for 125V, single-phase, 15A and 20A receptacles in pits, hoistways, on cars, and in wellways and machinery spaces.

sections.title: GFCI protection in elevator spaces
sections.plain_explanation:
620.6 puts GFCI protection where elevator work puts people in contact with water, grounded metal and machinery:
• All 125V, single-phase, 15A and 20A receptacles installed in pits, in hoistways, on elevator and dumbwaiter cars, in escalator and moving-walk wellways, and in the runways and machinery spaces of platform lifts and stairway chairlifts must be of the GFCI type — the protection is at the receptacle, not just a GFCI breaker upstream.
• Receptacles in machine rooms, control rooms, machinery spaces and control spaces must also have GFCI protection for personnel.
• A permanently installed sump pump in the pit must be permanently wired or supplied by a single GFCI-protected receptacle — the blanket sump-pump exemption as printed in the 2017 edition is gone in 2020.
sections.on_the_job: Small medical office in Orlando, two-stop elevator: Sharma's scope is the pit and machine-room receptacles. The crew installs GFCI receptacles — not a breaker alone — at the pit and hoistway locations, and the pit sump pump goes on a single GFCI-protected receptacle instead of being treated as exempt. One caution stays in the estimate notes: the 2020 Handbook notes the hard-wired sump-pump wording sits awkwardly with 422.5(A)(6), so that detail is worth an AHJ conversation on a real job before rough-in.
sections.figure_idea: Pit receptacle with the GFCI device at the outlet, sump pump on a single protected receptacle.
sections.why_it_exists: The pit is the worst receptacle location in the building: standing water, a sump, grounded rails and car metal on every side, and a technician working on a ladder or kneeling in the damp. A tool or trouble light that faults there puts current through the worker to the rails. GFCI protection at the outlet trips in milliseconds, before that fault becomes a fatality.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is protecting the pit receptacle with a GFCI breaker in the panel and calling it done. For pits, hoistways, cars and wellways, 620.6 requires receptacles of the GFCI type — the device is at the outlet. The second trap is 2017 habit: the blanket sump-pump exemption is gone in 2020, so an unprotected pit sump pump fails.
inspection_fails: Pit receptacle is a standard receptacle fed from a GFCI breaker — 620.6 requires the GFCI type at the receptacle in pits and hoistways.
Pit sump pump plugged into an unprotected receptacle with the old exemption claimed — the 2017 blanket exemption is gone in 2020.
Machine room receptacles installed with no GFCI protection for personnel.

figures.alt: Elevator pit elevation with the car above, a GFCI-type receptacle on the pit wall, and a sump pump in its recess on a single GFCI-protected receptacle, with a red panel showing that a plain receptacle on a GFCI breaker alone fails in the pit.
figures.caption: In the pit, the GFCI device is at the receptacle — and the sump pump is protected too.

page_quiz.question: A receptacle installed in an elevator pit must be:
choices: A standard receptacle on a GFCI breaker
page_quiz.explain_plain: For pits, hoistways, cars and wellways, 620.6 requires the receptacle itself to be of the GFCI type — upstream breaker protection alone is not the rule there.

page_quiz.question: A permanently installed sump pump in an elevator pit, under the 2020 NEC:
choices: Must be permanently wired or supplied by a single GFCI-protected receptacle
Must be cord-and-plug on a standard receptacle
page_quiz.explain_plain: The blanket sump-pump exemption printed in the 2017 edition is gone in 2020; the pump is hardwired or on one GFCI-protected receptacle.

page_quiz.question: Receptacles in elevator machine rooms and control spaces need:
page_quiz.explain_plain: 620.6 also requires GFCI protection for personnel on receptacles in machine rooms, control rooms, machinery spaces and control spaces.

sections.title: Car lighting, receptacle, ventilation, heating and air-conditioning branch circuits
sections.plain_explanation:
This section puts the car loads on their own dedicated circuits, apart from the driving-machine supply.
• 620.22(A): a separate branch circuit supplies the car lights, receptacle(s), auxiliary lighting power source, and ventilation on each car. The required car lighting must not be connected to the load side of a GFCI — a tripped service receptacle must not black out the car.
• 620.22(B): car heating and air-conditioning units are supplied by their own separate branch circuit.
The overcurrent device protecting each circuit is located in the machine room or control space for that car, and neither circuit is opened by the driving-machine disconnect (620.51), so the car stays lit and ventilated while the machine is locked out for service.
sections.on_the_job: Small commercial job — a two-stop elevator in a Florida medical office. Sharma runs two dedicated 20 A circuits to each car from the machine-room panel: the first for the car lights, the car receptacle, and ventilation; the second for the car heating and air-conditioning unit alone. Both breakers live in the machine room, where the inspector looks for them. The car receptacle is a GFCI type (620.6), wired so its load terminals never feed the car lights — a receptacle trip leaves the car lit.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: The mechanic servicing the driving machine locks out the machine disconnect — and is often standing in the car or the hoistway when he does it. If that disconnect also killed the car lights and ventilation, he would be working in a dark, unventilated shaft. The same thinking keeps the car lighting off the load side of a GFCI: one tripped receptacle must not strand passengers in a black car between floors.
inspection_fails: Car lights, receptacle and ventilation combined with the car heating and air-conditioning on one branch circuit (620.22(B)).
Required car lighting fed from the load side of a GFCI, so a receptacle trip blacks out the car (620.22(A)).
Car circuit breakers located in the car or at the service instead of in the machine room or control space for that car.
Car circuits opened by the driving-machine disconnect (620.51) — the car goes dark when the machine is locked out.
Non-GFCI receptacle installed on the car, in the pit, or in the machine room (620.6).
sections.exam_trap: The common wrong answer is one circuit for everything in the car — lights, receptacle, ventilation and the AC on a single 20 A run, because it is all 'car load.' 620.22(B) wants the heating and air-conditioning on their own separate branch circuit. Second trap: feeding the car lights through the load side of the car's GFCI receptacle — convenient, and exactly what 620.22(A) forbids.

page_quiz.question: Car heating and air-conditioning units must be supplied by:
choices: The same circuit as the car lights
page_quiz.explain_plain: 620.22(B) puts car heating and AC on a separate branch circuit of their own.

page_quiz.question: The required car lighting must NOT be connected to:
choices: The load side of a GFCI
page_quiz.explain_plain: If the car lighting sat on the load side of a GFCI, a tripped service receptacle would black out the car.

page_quiz.question: Where is the overcurrent device for each car branch circuit located?
choices: In the car, beside the operating panel
In the machine room or control space for that car
page_quiz.explain_plain: Both car circuits are protected from the machine room or control space, and neither is opened by the 620.51 disconnect.

sections.title: Disconnecting means — one per unit, lockable open only
sections.plain_explanation:
Each elevator, dumbwaiter, escalator, moving walk, platform lift, or stairway chairlift gets its own disconnecting means: an enclosed, externally operable fused motor-circuit switch or circuit breaker that disconnects the driving machine.
• One disconnect per unit — two machines never share one.
• The disconnect must be lockable in the open position only. It is not permitted to be lockable in the closed position.
• It must not disconnect the car lighting, receptacle, and ventilation circuits covered by 620.22, 620.23, and 620.24. Those stay energized so service work in the car is not done in the dark.
sections.on_the_job: Two elevators in a Winter Park medical office: each machine room disconnect is its own enclosed switch, labeled for its unit — 'ELEVATOR 1', 'ELEVATOR 2' — and each locks open with the mechanic's padlock. The car light and ventilation breaker sits in its own enclosure beside them and stays on while a machine is locked out, so the tech in the car keeps light and air. One disconnect per unit, labeled, and never let it kill the car light circuit — a serviceman in a dark car is exactly what the rule prevents.
sections.figure_idea: Machine-room disconnect with lock hasp in the open position only; car-light circuit breaker in a separate enclosure.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: The lock tells the story. A mechanic working on a machine locks the disconnect open so nobody can re-energize it mid-job — and the code forbids a lock in the closed position so the switch can never be locked ON against the mechanic. At the same time, killing the machine must not strand a second worker in a dark, unventilated car, which is why the car circuits live outside this disconnect.
inspection_fails: One disconnect feeding two driving machines.
Disconnect that can be locked in the closed position.
Machine disconnect also kills the car lighting and ventilation circuits.
Disconnect not identified for its unit in a multi-car machine room.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is the fire pump habit: a 695 disconnect is lockable in the CLOSED position so nobody can casually shut the pump off. Article 620 wants the exact opposite — lockable open only, never lockable closed. Picking 'lockable in the closed position' on a 620.51 question imports the wrong article's rule.

page_quiz.question: Each 620.51 disconnecting means must be lockable in:
page_quiz.explain_plain: Lockable in the open position only; it is not permitted to be lockable in the closed position.

page_quiz.question: The 620.51 disconnect must NOT disconnect:
choices: Car lighting, receptacle and ventilation circuits
page_quiz.explain_plain: The 620.22, 620.23 and 620.24 car circuits are arranged to stay energized for service work.

page_quiz.explain_plain: Each unit gets its own disconnecting means.

sections.title: Selective coordination
sections.plain_explanation:
Where one feeder supplies more than one elevator driving machine, the overcurrent device in each machine's disconnecting means must be selectively coordinated with any other supply-side overcurrent device. Coordinated means a fault at one machine opens only that machine's device — the feeder device and the other machines' devices hold, so one fault does not strand every car on the feeder.
• The rule is triggered by the arrangement: two or more driving machine disconnecting means supplied by a single feeder.
• The selection must be made by a licensed professional engineer, or by another qualified person engaged primarily in the design, installation, or maintenance of electrical systems.
• The selection — including the device settings, a documentation point the 2020 edition added — must be documented and made available to those authorized to design, install, inspect, maintain, and operate the system.
• Enclosures containing selectively coordinated devices are marked per 620.65.
sections.on_the_job: Two-car bank in a Winter Park medical office. One feeder from the switchboard supplies both machine disconnects, so 620.62 applies. Sharma's scope is the feeder and the two disconnects — Siemens gear, as always on new work — but the coordination is an engineering deliverable, not a field decision. Get the documented study, with the device settings, into the job file before trim-out, and confirm the enclosures carry the 620.65 marking. An inspector who asks for the study and hears "the elevator vendor is sending it" writes it up.
sections.figure_idea: Two elevator disconnects on one feeder with the coordination study folder in the machine room.
sections.why_it_exists: A car stalled between floors is an inconvenience. Every car in the bank dark and dead because one motor faulted is an entrapment problem: passengers stuck in all of them, and no working car to move people or bring up tools. Coordination keeps a single fault local, so the healthy machines keep running while the faulted one is repaired.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: "Selective coordination is only an Article 700 emergency-system rule." Wrong — 620.62 requires it on an ordinary elevator feeder that supplies more than one driving machine, in a building with no emergency system at all. The second trap is treating coordination as a field adjustment: the installer does not dial it in. A licensed PE or other qualified person selects it, and the settings are documented.

Documented; available to AHJ and O&M

Enclosure containing coordinated devices not marked per 620.65.
Feeder breaker trips on a single-car fault and strands both cars — the devices were never coordinated.

page_quiz.explain_plain: Each machine disconnect's overcurrent device must be selectively coordinated with any other supply-side overcurrent device.

choices: A licensed professional engineer or other qualified person engaged primarily in electrical design, installation, or maintenance
page_quiz.explain_plain: The selection is an engineering act, made by a licensed PE or other qualified person, and it must be documented.

sections.title: Article 625 — Electric Vehicle Power Transfer System
sections.plain_explanation:
The 2020 edition renamed this article from 'Charging System' to 'Power Transfer System' because the equipment now moves power both ways — charging, power export, and bidirectional flow are all inside the article's scope. The field core for Sharma:
• One dedicated branch circuit for each EV outlet (625.40) — no sharing with other loads.
• EV charging is a continuous load, so overcurrent protection and conductors are sized at 125 percent (625.41, 625.42).
• A lockable disconnect where the equipment is rated over 60 A or over 150 V to ground (625.43).
• GFCI protection for personnel on every receptacle installed for EV charging (625.54) — the EVSE's own internal protection does not take its place.
• The output cable to the vehicle is limited to 25 ft of overall usable length unless the listed equipment includes a cable management system (625.17(B)(3)); power-supply cords on cord-and-plug EVSE have their own length limits.
A longer cord draped across a garage floor or a parking space is a trip hazard and a listing problem at the same time — plan the charger location so 25 ft reaches the charge port of the vehicles the space serves.
sections.on_the_job: A Winter Park garage gets a 48 A hardwired EVSE. Continuous load, so the branch circuit is 48 × 1.25 = 60 A — one dedicated circuit for that one outlet (625.40) out of a new Siemens panel, and the wall unit is placed so its 25 ft output cable reaches the charge ports on both parking spots without crossing the walk-door path. Garage EV points follow Sharma's garage rules (S-07, S-01) only where they don't conflict with Article 625 — the article wins where they differ.
sections.figure_idea: Garage wall with a hardwired EVSE on its own circuit; bidirectional unit exporting to a house panel shown in a second panel of the figure.
sections.florida_note: Florida enforces NEC 2020 through the Florida Building Code 8th Edition (2023), for permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026; the FBC 9th Edition (2026) adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026. The NEC 2023 changes in this article apply in Florida to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026 (FBC 9th Ed.); earlier permits stay on NEC 2020.

sections.why_it_exists: A charger pulls its full rating for hours at a time — a steady load, more like a range that never cycles off. Shared circuits, 100 percent sizing and cords stretched across walk paths turn that draw into heat and trip hazards. The article answers with a dedicated circuit per outlet, 125 percent sizing, GFCI protection and a hard limit on cable length.
inspection_fails: EV outlet sharing a branch circuit with other loads — 625.40 requires an individual branch circuit for each EV outlet.
Charger circuit sized at 100 percent of nameplate; EV charging is a continuous load at 125 percent (625.41, 625.42).
Receptacle installed for EV charging with no GFCI protection for personnel (625.54).
Output cable longer than 25 ft with no listed cable management system (625.17(B)(3)).
Equipment over 60 A or 150 V to ground with no lockable disconnect (625.43).
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating a bidirectional EVSE as outside the article because 'it exports instead of charging.' The 2020 rename to Power Transfer System was deliberate — export and bidirectional equipment sit inside Article 625. Answering 'charging rules do not apply' is the wrong answer.

sections.title: Electric vehicle branch circuit — one outlet, one circuit
sections.plain_explanation:
In NEC 2020 the rule is flat: each outlet installed for the purpose of charging an electric vehicle must be supplied by an individual branch circuit, and that circuit must have no other outlets.
• It applies to every EV charging outlet, whatever its size — there is no small-charger carve-out in the 2020 text.
• A 240 V wall connector, a 14-50 receptacle installed for charging, and a 120 V outlet installed for Level 1 charging each get their own circuit.
• Sharing happens upstream, not here: listed load management under 625.42 can cap what several chargers draw from a service or feeder, but each outlet still lands on its own branch circuit.
sections.on_the_job: Two-car garage in Winter Park: the owners run two 48 A wall connectors. Under Florida's 2020 rules that is two circuits — a 60 A individual branch circuit to each charger (48 A × 125% per 625.41), two home runs, two breakers, nothing else on either one. The chargers talk to each other and share the service through load management (625.42), which is legal because the sharing happens upstream of the branch circuits, not by doubling up an outlet.

The NEC 2023 changes in this article apply in Florida to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026 (FBC 9th Ed.); earlier permits stay on NEC 2020.

sections.why_it_exists: A charger is a continuous load that can pull its full rating for hours. Two chargers doubled onto one circuit means conductors and a breaker sized for one car carrying two — nuisance trips at best, cooked insulation at worst. One outlet per circuit also means one fault or one bad charger never takes out the other car.

Both statements belong to NEC 2023, which Florida applies only to permits filed on or after Dec 31, 2026. On a 2020 exam — and on a 2020 permit — every EV outlet gets an individual branch circuit with no other outlets, full stop.

sections.title: Overcurrent protection — 125% of maximum load
sections.plain_explanation:
EV charging is a continuous load — a charger can pull its full rating for three hours or more on an overnight charge. So the overcurrent device protecting a feeder or branch circuit that supplies EV charging is sized at not less than 125% of the equipment's maximum load, and the conductors are sized to the same figure (625.42).
• 32 A charger → 125% is 40 A → a 40 A breaker.
• 40 A charger → 125% is 50 A → a 50 A breaker.
• 48 A charger → 125% is 60 A → a 60 A breaker.
Size from the charger's maximum setting, not from the car plugged in today and not from a lower setting picked in an app. Where access to the adjustment is restricted, or a listed load management system caps the load, 625.42 lets the service and feeder be figured at the capped load — but each EV outlet still gets its own branch circuit (625.40).
sections.on_the_job: Two-car garage in Orlando on a 200 A Siemens panel. One side is a plug-in charger set to 40 A on a 240 V receptacle: 40 × 1.25 = 50, so it lands on a 50 A two-pole GFCI breaker — 625.54 requires GFCI protection for the charging receptacle — with 8 AWG copper, good for 50 A at 75 °C. The other side is a hardwired unit set to 48 A: 48 × 1.25 = 60, a 60 A breaker, and the wire steps up to 6 AWG copper because 8 AWG stops at 50 A. The panel schedule is written from the chargers' maximum settings, not from the two cars that happen to live there now.
sections.figure_idea: Breaker schedule callout: 48A EVSE → 60A breaker, conductor sized to match.
sections.why_it_exists: A breaker and its conductors sized at exactly 100% of a load that runs all night sit at their thermal edge for hours at a time. Breakers trip on heat, terminations loosen and cook over repeated long cycles, and insulation ages fast when it runs hot. The 125% factor is the Code's continuous-load margin: it keeps the device, the lugs and the wire in their comfortable range for the whole charge, every night, for years.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing from the setting on the screen: 'the charger is set to 32 A, so a 40 A breaker is plenty' — until the owner raises it to 48 A in the app and the 40 A breaker cooks every night. Unless the adjustment is restricted the way 625.42 requires, the maximum load is the equipment's maximum setting. The other trap is a 48 A charger on a 50 A breaker because a 50 A receptacle was handy: 50 is less than 60, and the math fails before the receptacle question even starts.

tables.caption: 625.41 sizing: charger maximum → breaker and wire
tables.note: Conductor ampacities from Table 310.16, copper, 75 °C column. Conductors are sized to the same 125% figure as the breaker (625.42).

inspection_fails: 48 A charger protected by a 50 A breaker — 125% of the maximum load is 60 A (625.41).
Charger circuit sized from the car's current charge setting instead of the equipment's maximum setting.
Two EV outlets sharing one branch circuit — each EV outlet gets its own circuit (625.40).
60 A breaker landed on 8 AWG copper — conductor ampacity (50 A at 75 °C) is below the 125% load figure.
EV charging receptacle with no GFCI protection (625.54).

sections.title: Rating — charging is a continuous load; load management
sections.plain_explanation:
Two ideas live in this section:
• EV charging is a continuous load. That single fact drives the 125% sizing of branch-circuit conductors and overcurrent devices in 625.41.
• Load management changes the math upstream. Where a listed automatic load management system is used, the maximum equipment load on a service or feeder is the maximum load the system permits — the managed cap, not the sum of every charger's nameplate. Equipment with adjustable settings is figured at its setting only where the adjustment means meets the section's conditions.
What load management never does: it does not merge branch circuits. Each outlet keeps its own circuit under 625.40, sized at 125% of that charger's maximum load.
sections.on_the_job: Orlando house, 200 A service, two 48 A chargers. Unmanaged, the pair is 96 A of nameplate — 120 A once the 125% continuous factor lands — on top of the house load. With a listed load management system capped at 80 A combined, the service and feeder are figured at 80 A for the EV load. Each charger still gets its own 60 A branch circuit (48 A × 125%), because 625.40 and 625.41 do not bend. The chargers slow down when the AC and range run together, and speed back up overnight.
sections.figure_idea: Load management controller capping two chargers at a combined service figure.

nec2023_change.change: The two ways to size services and feeders below the nameplate, load management and restricted adjustable settings, now sit in 625.42(A) and (B) and tie to the energy management rules in 750.30. Every EV charger counts as a continuous load, so size its circuit conductors and overcurrent device at 125 percent of the rating.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 625.42 EV charger rating and load management

sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 625.42: The two ways to size services and feeders below the nameplate, load management and restricted adjustable settings, now sit in 625.42(A) and (B) and tie to the energy management rules in 750.30. Every EV charger counts as a continuous load, so size its circuit conductors and overcurrent device at 125 percent of the rating.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Services in Florida homes were not built for two cars charging all night on top of air conditioning. Without the continuous-load rule, breakers and conductors would cook at full rating for hours. Load management is the release valve: a listed system watches the service and throttles the chargers, so the house can charge both cars without a service upgrade — while the cap, not wishful thinking, becomes the number the service is sized on.
inspection_fails: Service calculation uses the sum of charger nameplates even though a listed load management system caps the load — or uses a cap from an unlisted add-on.
Adjustable charger figured at a low app setting with no restricted adjustment means.
EV load figured as noncontinuous; branch-circuit breaker trips on long overnight charges.
One branch circuit split between two chargers, justified by the load manager.
sections.exam_trap: The classic wrong answer: 'the load manager caps the pair at 80 A, so run one 80 A circuit and split it between both chargers.' Load management caps the service and feeder figure only. The branch circuits stay individual and stay sized at 125% of each charger's maximum. The second trap is figuring an adjustable charger at the low setting a homeowner picked in an app — the setting counts only when the adjustment means meets the section's conditions.

sections.title: Disconnecting means — over 60A or 150V to ground
sections.plain_explanation:
EV charging equipment rated more than 60 A, or more than 150 V to ground, needs its own disconnecting means under this section:
• The disconnect must be readily accessible — reachable quickly, without climbing over or moving anything.
• It must be capable of being locked in the open position, and the locking provision stays in place whether the lock is on it or not, as 110.25 requires.
• Equipment rated at or under both thresholds — 60 A or less and 150 V or less to ground — does not need the separate disconnect under 625.43.
The rating that counts is the equipment's rating, not the size of the breaker feeding it. A 48 A charger on a 60 A circuit is still 48 A equipment.
sections.why_it_exists: Big chargers move enough energy to hurt someone fast, and their electronics can leave parts energized after the vehicle is unplugged. A lockable disconnect within reach lets a technician, a firefighter, or the building owner kill the equipment for certain and keep it dead while hands are inside it. The lock is what turns “somebody switched it off” into “it stays off until I say so.”
sections.on_the_job: Fleet depot in Lakeland: two DC fast chargers rated 100 A each. Both are over the 60 A threshold, so each gets a lockable disconnect on the wall beside it, readily accessible from the drive aisle — planned at rough-in, while the wall is open and the gear layout can still move, not discovered at the final. Across the lot, the employee chargers are 48 A wall units on 60 A circuits: the equipment rating is under 60 A, so 625.43 does not force a separate disconnect for them. Same article, two answers — the nameplate decides.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is rating the circuit instead of the equipment: a 48 A charger on a 60 A breaker does not trip this rule, and a charger rated exactly 60 A does not either — the section starts at MORE THAN 60 A. The second trap is a disconnect that can only be locked with a removable hasp kept in the truck: 110.25 wants the locking provision to remain in place with the lock removed.

tables.caption: When 625.43 requires the disconnect
rows: 60 A or less and 150 V or less to ground
tables.note: The 2023 plaque rule for remote disconnects is in the 2020 vs 2023 box.

Disconnect fitted with a locking hasp that lives in the gang box; nothing left to lock to once it walks off (110.25).
Disconnect mounted behind the charger's bollards, where nobody can stand in front of it and reach the handle.
Lockable disconnect installed, but on the far side of a locked fence the service technician cannot open.

sections.title: Equipment connections — how the charger plugs in
sections.plain_explanation:
625.44 sorts electric vehicle equipment by how it connects to the premises wiring, and each style carries its own connection rule.
• Portable equipment connects cord-and-plug through a receptacle.
• Stationary equipment may also be cord-and-plug connected where the section permits it.
• Fastened-in-place equipment has its own provisions, including direct wiring.
Where a receptacle is the connection, it must be a listed receptacle of the rating and configuration the equipment requires — the charger nameplate, not habit, picks the receptacle. The dwelling case crews see most is a 240-volt receptacle feeding a plug-in charger: the receptacle rating, the branch-circuit rating, and the charger's continuous draw all have to agree, which is why this section is read together with 625.41 and 625.42.
sections.on_the_job: Plug-in charger on a 50 A receptacle: the circuit is sized for the continuous load at 125 percent (a 40 A charger on a 50 A circuit), the receptacle matches the circuit, and the equipment is the listed unit the homeowner bought — not a dryer receptacle borrowed for the garage. If the charger is hard-wired instead, 625.44 steps aside and the disconnect rules of 625.43 decide.
sections.figure_idea: Three connection styles side by side: portable cord-and-plug, stationary cord-and-plug, fastened-in-place direct-wired.

sections.why_it_exists: A charger draws its full rating for hours. A receptacle chosen by habit — the dryer-style outlet that happens to be in the garage — can be the wrong configuration, the wrong rating, or fed by a circuit never sized for a continuous load. Matching the receptacle, the circuit and the nameplate keeps the connection from becoming the hot spot in the system.

sections.title: Connector storage — 18 in. indoors, 24 in. outdoors
sections.plain_explanation:
Unless the equipment is listed and marked for a different arrangement, the coupling means — the vehicle connector — must be stored or located at a height of:
• Not less than 18 in. above the floor for indoor locations.
• Not less than 24 in. above grade for outdoor locations.
It also has to be positioned so it can couple directly to the vehicle: stored where the cord actually reaches the charge port, not coiled on a hook across the garage. The heights are minimums, and they are measured to where the connector sits in its holster or storage position.
sections.on_the_job: Florida makes this one easy to get wrong. A wall charger inside a garage gets its holster mounted so the connector docks at 18 in. or more above the slab — above the water line when the floor is hosed out or a storm blows rain under the door. The same charger on an outside wall or a carport post is an outdoor location: 24 in. minimum above grade, because an afternoon storm can pond water against that wall in minutes. Measure to where the connector actually sits docked, not to the top of the holster bracket.
sections.figure_idea: Connector docked in its holster at compliant height, indoor and outdoor versions.
sections.why_it_exists: A connector stored down at floor level lives in the worst spot in the building: garage floor water, driveway runoff, tire paths and dropped tools. Water and grit in the connector contacts corrode them, and a damaged connector can damage the vehicle's inlet too. The minimum heights keep the coupling means out of standing water and out from under tires.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is carrying the indoor number outside: 18 in. is the indoor floor measurement. Outdoors the minimum is 24 in., measured from grade — not from the driveway's high spot or the top of a paver. The second trap is measuring to the holster's mounting screws instead of to the stored connector itself; the rule is about where the coupling means sits.

page_quiz.question: A vehicle connector stored indoors must be located at least ___ above the floor.
page_quiz.explain_plain: Indoors the minimum is 18 in. above the floor.

sections.title: Ventilation — only where the listing requires it
sections.plain_explanation:
Indoor EV charging needs mechanical ventilation only where the listing says so:
• Equipment listed as requiring ventilation for indoor use: mechanical ventilation is required.
• Equipment listed for indoor charging without ventilation: none is required — most modern residential EVSE is listed this way.
• Where ventilation is required, it is a permanent system: supply air and exhaust, vented directly to the outdoors, arranged for the vehicles being charged.
The listing and the installation instructions are the rule here — equipment is installed per its listing (110.3(B)), and 625.52 keys the ventilation question to that listing.
sections.on_the_job: Garage install in a Florida home: a 48 A wall-mounted EVSE on a 60 A circuit (625.41) — the nameplate and instructions say listed for indoor use, no ventilation required. The crew prices no ductwork, and notes the listing line on the work order so the inspector sees the basis at rough-in. Across town, a fleet shop buys chargers whose listing requires ventilation for indoor use: that job carries a permanent supply-and-exhaust system vented straight outdoors, priced before the chargers are mounted.
sections.figure_idea: Garage charger shown twice: listed 'no ventilation required' vs. a vented commercial installation.
sections.why_it_exists: Some charging equipment and battery chemistries can give off gases while charging, and in a closed garage those gases must not be allowed to build up. Equipment listed for indoor use without ventilation has that hazard engineered out, so the Code does not make every garage charger carry ductwork it does not need — the ventilation follows the listing, not a blanket rule.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is the blanket answer — every indoor EV charger needs mechanical ventilation. 625.52 requires ventilation only where the equipment is listed as requiring it for indoor use. The reverse trap also fails jobs: skipping ventilation where the listing does require it, or offering a portable fan where a permanent supply-and-exhaust system vented outdoors is required.

Exhaust dumped into the attic instead of vented directly to the outdoors.

sections.title: GFCI protection for personnel — every EV receptacle
sections.plain_explanation:
All receptacles installed for the connection of electric vehicle charging must be provided with GFCI protection for personnel:
• The requirement is in addition to the dwelling garage rules in 210.8 — it stands on its own.
• A 240 V charging receptacle is not exempt.
• Indoor locations are not exempt.
• The charger receptacle is the outlet being protected. The EVSE's own internal personnel protection system does not substitute for the required GFCI protection.
If a receptacle exists to plug in a charger, 625.54 protects it — the voltage and the room do not matter.
sections.why_it_exists: A charge cord lives a hard life: driven over, kinked, rained on, and plugged in with wet hands on a concrete slab. A ground fault through a damaged cord or a wet connector puts current through the person holding it, and a 50 A breaker will never notice a few milliamperes going the wrong way. GFCI protection watches for current leaking where it should not go and opens the circuit fast — that is the difference between a scare and a fatality.
sections.on_the_job: Spec home in Ocala: the garage gets a 240 V, 50 A receptacle for the buyer's charger, fed from the Siemens panel on a 2-pole GFCI breaker — 50 A because the 40 A charger is a continuous load under 625.41. The receptacle itself is a standard heavy-duty 14-50; the protection lives in the breaker, and the crew labels the receptacle “EV charging — GFCI protected” so the inspector and the homeowner both see it. Per the Sharma note on this page, the 240 V circuit is not an S-07 dual-function point — S-07 is a 120 V device rule — so nobody specs a dual-function breaker here; the listed 2-pole GFCI breaker is the protection method for this job.
sections.exam_trap: Two traps. First: “the EVSE already has personnel protection built in, so the receptacle needs nothing.” 625.54 protects the receptacle, and the charger's internal system does not substitute for it. Second: “GFCI is only for 120 V receptacles.” This section covers every receptacle installed for EV charging, 240 V included, indoors or out.

sections.title: Wet location — weatherproof enclosure
sections.plain_explanation:
625.56 is one sentence long: receptacles installed outdoors or in wet locations for EV charging must be enclosed so the enclosure is weatherproof with the attachment plug cap inserted or removed. In plain terms, weatherproof while in use — the same duty other outdoor receptacles carry under 406.9(B)(1).
• A standard flip cover is weatherproof only with nothing plugged in. It fails this rule the moment a charge cord is connected.
• The cover that passes is an in-use ('bubble') cover: a deep hood that closes over the plug and cord for the whole charge.
• The receptacle still owes GFCI protection for personnel under 625.54. The cover and the GFCI are separate duties — one does not excuse the other.
sections.on_the_job: Florida spec home with the charger receptacle on the driveway wall: a 240 V, 50 A receptacle on GFCI protection (625.54) with a bubble cover over it, so the EVSE plug stays dry through an afternoon thunderstorm in the middle of a charge. Sharma standard: put the in-use cover on the rough-in material list for every outdoor charger receptacle — standard flip covers don't meet in-use duty, and swapping a cover after final is a callback, not a change order.
sections.figure_idea: Outdoor receptacle with an in-use cover, charger plugged in, cover closed.

sections.why_it_exists: An outdoor EV receptacle stays plugged in for hours, usually unattended and often overnight, through Florida rain. A cover that only works with nothing plugged in protects the receptacle exactly when it is not being used. Water tracking into a live receptacle corrodes the contacts, builds leakage paths and can energize the enclosure — the in-use cover keeps the weather out for the entire charge.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is 'weatherproof means a flip cover.' A flip cover is weatherproof with the plug removed; 625.56 requires weatherproof with the plug inserted OR removed. The other wrong answer is that the EVSE's own internal protection covers the receptacle — it does not substitute for the 625.54 GFCI, and it does nothing for the 625.56 enclosure duty.
inspection_fails: Flip cover on an outdoor EV receptacle — not weatherproof while the charger is plugged in.
In-use cover too shallow for the plug, left propped open so the hood cannot close.
Outdoor charging receptacle with no GFCI protection for personnel (625.54).
Receptacle enclosure open to driven rain at the conduit entry — the cover is right, the box is not weatherproof.

choices: In-use (bubble) cover that closes over the plug
No cover if under a carport roof
page_quiz.explain_plain: Only an in-use cover stays weatherproof with the charger plugged in.

sections.title: Article 626 — Electrified Truck Parking Spaces
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 626 covers electrified truck parking spaces: the pedestals, receptacles, and disconnects that let a parked truck run cab heat, air conditioning, and appliances — and a refrigerated trailer keep its load cold — without idling the engine. The article covers the equipment external to the truck. The numbers that drive a bid:
• 626.11(A) — every space is figured at not less than 11 kVA in feeder and service load calculations, before the climate-zone demand factors of 626.11(B). The 11 kVA is built from the receptacles each space must have: two 20 A, 120 V receptacles plus one 30 A, 208 V circuit.
• 626.24(B) — each space's connection means provides at least three receptacles, on at least two different branch circuits, and the receptacles get GFCI protection (626.24(D)).
• 626.22 — supply equipment on a pedestal or raised pad mounts at least 2 ft above grade, or above the high-water mark where flooding reaches, and a remote disconnecting means that can be locked in the open position kills the supply to one or more spaces.
• 626.10 — each stand is supplied from a 208Y/120 V or 480Y/277 V system.
Where Article 626 conflicts with another article, 626.3 says Article 626 applies.
sections.why_it_exists: A diesel idling all night burns fuel, makes noise, and wears the engine — shore power is the clean answer, but it puts a serious continuous load in a parking lot full of fuel, water, and road salt. Pedestals get hit, cords get driven over, and drivers plug in during rainstorms. The receptacle, GFCI, mounting-height, and lockable-disconnect rules are written for equipment that lives outdoors and gets abused.
sections.on_the_job: Distribution warehouse in Polk County adds six electrified spaces for overnight tractors. The load math starts at 6 × 11 kVA = 66 kVA before the 626.11(B) climate-zone demand factors — a real feeder, not a site-lighting tap — so the pedestals get their own panel and a disconnect that locks open for the row. Each pedestal mounts at least 2 ft above grade (the lot ponds in summer storms), carries the 626.24(B) receptacle set with GFCI protection, and is priced from the pedestal schedule: spaces counted, receptacle types confirmed, disconnect per the layout. Treat each pedestal like a small service with its own grounding, exactly as the old note on this page said — now with the article's numbers filled in.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing a space like a 20 A convenience receptacle. 626.11(A) fixes the floor at 11 kVA per space before demand factors, and the branch-circuit loads are continuous. Second trap: applying another article over 626 where the two conflict — 626.3 gives the tie to Article 626 on its own turf.

sections.title: Article 630 — Electric Welders
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 630 gives electric welders their own conductor and overcurrent rules, because a welder welds in bursts and rests between welds. The whole article runs on one nameplate number: the duty cycle.
• Duty cycle is the share of time the machine can weld at rated output — 60 percent means about 6 minutes welding out of every 10 at that output.
• Supply conductors: ampacity not less than the I1eff value on the rating plate. If the plate gives no I1eff, multiply the rated primary current by the Table 630.11(A) factor for that duty cycle (630.11(A)).
• Motor-generator arc welders use their own column of Table 630.11(A). Resistance welders follow Part III instead (630.31).
• A group of welders on one feeder: 100 percent of the two largest, plus 85 percent of the third largest, plus 70 percent of the fourth, plus 60 percent of all the rest (630.11(B)).
• Overcurrent protection is generous on purpose: not more than 200 percent of the rated primary current, and not more than 200 percent of the conductor ampacity (630.12).
• Shop work: get the duty cycle off the nameplate before sizing anything. Never guess it.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: a welder with a 50 A rated primary current at a 60 percent duty cycle takes the 630.11(A) multiplier of 0.78 for a nonmotor-generator arc welder (motor-generator welders use a different column), so its supply conductors need an ampacity of at least 50 × 0.78 = 39 A. Read the duty cycle off the nameplate every time, not guessed. On a fabrication-shop job off OBT adding a welder bay, that one calculation sets the whole circuit: conductors at 39 A minimum ampacity, and a breaker that may run well above the conductor size, up to the 630.12 ceiling of 200 percent of 50 A — 100 A. Show the duty-cycle math on the panel schedule so the inspector sees Article 630, not a mistake.

nec2023_change.change: Created a new Section 630.8 requiring ground-fault circuit-interrupter (GFCI) protection for personnel involved with electric welder applications.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 630.8 Ground-Fault Circuit-Interrupter Protection for Personnel (Electric Welders)

sections.why_it_exists: Conductor heating follows the current squared times the time it flows. A machine that rests between welds never heats its supply conductors the way a continuous load of the same nameplate current would. Sizing to full nameplate current wastes copper; sizing by guesswork cooks insulation. The duty-cycle table splits the difference with physics, and the 200 percent breaker ceiling exists so striking an arc does not nuisance-trip — the welder's own thermal protection guards the machine.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is protecting the welder circuit like an ordinary load: a breaker matched to the 39 A conductor ampacity, or conductors sized at the full 50 A nameplate. 630.12 keys the breaker ceiling to the rated primary current — up to 200 percent — not to the derated conductor size, and 630.11 keys the conductors to the duty cycle, not the nameplate.
inspection_fails: Welder circuit sized off the machine's output current (the 225 A on the front of a stick welder) instead of its rated primary current.
Breaker above 200 percent of the rated primary current — past the 630.12 ceiling.
Duty cycle guessed or taken from the sales sheet instead of the rating plate, leaving conductors undersized for the machine's actual cycle.
Welder tapped onto a general shop circuit with lighting and receptacles, with no 630.11 calculation behind it.

sections.title: Article 640 — Audio Signal Processing, Amplification, and Reproduction Equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 640 covers the power and wiring rules for audio signal processing, amplification and reproduction equipment — the professional and commercial sound systems in studios, performance venues, houses of worship and distributed-audio fit-outs.
• Line-voltage power to the equipment — the rack circuits — follows the general rules of Chapters 1 through 4 as Article 640 modifies them.
• The audio side — speaker wiring and signal cabling — follows Article 640's own wiring rules, and it is not interchangeable with line-voltage wiring.
• Most of the article lands on the specialty AV contractor. Sharma touches it when a commercial fit-out includes distributed audio and somebody has to feed the rack.
sections.on_the_job: A restaurant fit-out with distributed audio shows the split. Sharma's bid carries the rack power — two 20 A branch circuits to the AV rack location, the circuit size we install as a commercial minimum — and the AV contractor owns the speaker wiring, pulled and terminated under Article 640. Settle who owns what before rough-in: line-voltage power and low-voltage audio cable follow different rules and different trades' habits, and that split belongs in the bid, not in a change order at trim.
sections.why_it_exists: A sound system puts two very different kinds of wiring in the same rack and the same ceiling: 120 V power that can start a fire, and speaker cable carrying signals that pick up every bit of noise nearby. Run them like one system and you get hum in the speakers, line voltage where nobody expects it, and faults on cable that was never built for it. The article keeps the two sides separated and gives each its own rules.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating speaker cable like any other low-voltage wire that can ride along with power: 'it's only speaker wire — run it in the rack power conduit.' Article 640 gives the audio side its own wiring rules, and mixing the two sides in one raceway is exactly what the article is written to prevent. The scope trap runs the other way too: assuming the whole sound system is the AV contractor's problem when nobody has scoped the line-voltage rack power.

Sound system energized with the power side and the audio side roughed in as one system.

sections.title: Article 645 — Information Technology Equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 645 gives special wiring allowances to IT equipment rooms that meet the article's conditions — including wiring under raised floors and the room disconnecting means. The allowances apply only when every condition in 645.4 is met; otherwise Chapters 1–4 govern as usual.
The room-level items Sharma would actually wire:
• A disconnecting means for the IT equipment — and for the dedicated HVAC serving the room — with remote disconnect controls at approved locations, readily accessible in case of fire to authorized personnel and emergency responders (645.10(A))
• The HVAC disconnect must also cause required fire/smoke dampers to close
• Underfloor branch circuits run only in the wiring methods 645.5 permits
• 645.10 also allows the remote disconnect controls to cover designated zones within the room, and there is an exception for Critical Operations Data Systems
The disconnect button at the door is the visible part of this article on a data-room job, and its location is settled at rough-in, not at trim.
sections.on_the_job: Before using any 645 allowance — underfloor wiring, the room disconnect arrangement — verify the room meets every condition in 645.4: dedicated IT room, the required disconnecting means, separation, and fire protection as the article lists them. On a small commercial server-room rough-in, walk that list with the plans before a single underfloor circuit goes in. If one condition fails — the HVAC is shared with the office, say — wire the room under Chapters 1 through 4 like any other space, and price it that way.
sections.why_it_exists: A data room concentrates a building's most expensive energized equipment in one locked space. In a fire, responders need to kill the equipment, its dedicated HVAC, and close the dampers from an approved spot outside the smoke — without hunting for panels. The underfloor allowances are the trade: the room earns relaxed wiring methods only because it is dedicated, separated, and protected as a system.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is “the room has a raised floor and racks, so Article 645 applies.” A raised floor buys nothing by itself: the allowances switch on only when every 645.4 condition is met. Miss one condition and the underfloor wiring and the room disconnect arrangement were never permitted — the room is a Chapters 1–4 room.

Remote disconnect controls at a location that is not approved, or not readily accessible in a fire.
HVAC disconnect that does not close the required fire/smoke dampers.
Underfloor wiring methods outside the ones 645.5 permits.
