sections.title: Article 646 — Modular Data Centers
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 646 covers modular data centers: factory-built, prefabricated units rated 600 volts or less — an outer enclosure housing racks or cabinets of information technology equipment plus the support equipment, power distribution and cooling, that runs them. The article was added in the 2014 cycle; it is not new in 2020.
• A listed module is treated as listed equipment: it complies with the specific sections the article points to, and its internal wiring is the manufacturer's listing — the listing route commonly runs through UL's Subject 2755 outline for modular data centers. A module that is not listed must comply with Article 646 in full.
• 646.5: a nameplate on each enclosure gives the full-load current and the short-circuit current rating. Supply conductors are sized at not less than 125 percent of the nameplate full-load current.
• 646.9: flexible cords and cables listed for extra-hard usage may interconnect separate module enclosures — but may never connect a module to an external power source such as the building service.
• 646.18: space about electrical equipment inside the module complies with 110.26.
• 646.19: for equipment over 6 ft wide or deep, there is an entrance to and egress from the working space at each end, each at least 24 in. wide and 6½ ft high, with listed panic hardware or listed fire exit hardware. A single entrance is permitted only where 646.19(A) or (B) is met.
sections.on_the_job: Treat the module as listed equipment: Sharma's scope is the supply feeder, the disconnect, and the grounding connection landed on the module's marked terminals. Never field-modify the module's internal wiring to make a site condition fit — that is the manufacturer's listing you would be voiding. Worked example: a module lands on a pad behind a Winter Park warehouse with a nameplate full-load current of 160 A. The supply conductors are sized at 125 percent — 200 A minimum — before any other adjustment, and the feeder lands only on the marked supply terminals. The nameplate stays visible after the unit is set; if the pad layout parks it against a wall, that is a punch item, not a detail.

nec2023_change.change: The revision of Section 646.19 specifies the requirements for egress doors located in modular data centers.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 646.19 Entrance to and Egress from Working Space

sections.why_it_exists: A modular data center packs a room's worth of energized distribution into a steel box with room for one person to work. If a fault or fire starts at the far end, the only safe direction is out — which is why the article fixes the working space and the exits at the factory instead of leaving them to whoever sets the box on the pad.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is answering 646.19 with 110.26(C)(2): that trigger is 1200 A. Article 646's trigger is size — equipment over 6 ft wide or deep needs an entrance at each end whatever its ampere rating.
inspection_fails: Supply conductors sized at 100 percent of the nameplate full-load current instead of 125 percent (646.5).
Flexible cord used to connect a module to the building service instead of only interconnecting enclosures (646.9).
Nameplate blocked or facing a wall after the module is set, so its ratings cannot be read.
Field-modified internal wiring inside a listed module, voiding the listing.
Equipment over 6 ft wide with a single entrance and neither 646.19(A) nor (B) met.

sections.title: Article 647 — Sensitive Electronic Equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 647 covers a special power system for sensitive electronic equipment: a 120 V, single-phase system whose transformer secondary is center-tapped, with the center tap grounded, so each ungrounded leg sits at 60 V to ground while the voltage between the legs stays 120 V.
• The two legs are equal and opposite to ground — that balance is what cancels the ground noise that hums through audio and video work.
• The system has its own receptacle and grounding rules; receptacles are identified for this system so ordinary equipment is not plugged into it by mistake.
• It is rare, and it is always an engineered installation — nobody wires one from habit.
sections.on_the_job: If a studio or production client asks for 'clean power,' do not improvise a balanced 60/60 system in the field — it is an engineered installation with its own identified receptacles and grounding arrangement. Route the request to Mike for a design before anyone quotes it. And if you ever meter one that is already installed: each slot reads about 60 V to ground, and the two slots read 120 V to each other. On a normal circuit that reading means a lost neutral; on a 647 system it is exactly right.
sections.why_it_exists: Production audio and video gear picks up noise through its ground connections, and on a normal circuit that noise lands in the recording. With both legs balanced at 60 V to ground, noise coupled equally onto the two legs cancels instead of adding. The same balance is the hazard if it is improvised: a receptacle that looks normal but carries 60 V on both slots confuses the next person who meters it or plugs into it — which is why the system uses identified receptacles and an engineered design.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answers are 'a 60 V system' and 'wire it like a normal 120 V circuit.' It is a 120 V system — 120 V leg to leg — and neither leg is a grounded neutral you can treat like one. The field trap is worse: building a 'balanced' feed out of a standard transformer hookup because the client asked for clean power. Article 647 work is engineered, or it is not done.

Sensitive-equipment system installed without the grounding arrangement its design requires.

sections.title: Article 650 — Pipe Organs
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 650 covers the electrical circuits and parts of electrically operated pipe organs that control the sounding apparatus and the keyboards — the action system. Electronic organs are a different animal: 650.3 sends them to Article 640.
• 650.4: the action runs on dc from a transformer-type rectifier, and the dc potential must not exceed 30 volts.
• 650.5: the rectifier is bonded to the equipment grounding conductor under Article 250 — the case is grounded, the low-voltage output is the working circuit.
• 650.6(A): conductor minimums are tiny and specific — 28 AWG for electronic signal circuits, 26 AWG for electromagnetic valve supply and the like, and the main common-return conductor in the electromagnetic supply not less than 14 AWG.
• 650.6(B)–(D): conductors carry thermoplastic or thermosetting insulation, are cabled together outside the organ proper, and each cable gets an outer covering — flame-spread resistant where the cable is not in metal raceway.
• 650.7: cables are fastened in place, may attach directly to the organ structure, and must not lie in contact with other conductors.
• 650.8: circuits are arranged so the 26 AWG and 28 AWG conductors are protected by an overcurrent device rated not more than 6 amperes.
sections.on_the_job: On a church job with an organ, coordinate two separate scopes: the blower is an ordinary motor circuit under Article 430, and the low-voltage action wiring is the organ builder's listed system. Sharma's rough-in is the line-voltage side — a 20 A branch circuit to the blower disconnect and a 20 A circuit feeding the rectifier location the builder picks. Get the builder's power requirements before rough-in — organs are usually discovered in the attic conversation, not on the electrical drawings.
sections.why_it_exists: An organ action system is hundreds of hair-thin conductors bundled through a wooden chamber full of dust, bellows, and century-old timber. A short on an unfused 28 AWG conductor cannot trip a normal breaker — it just glows. The 30-volt cap, the 6-ampere fuse cap, and the cabling rules keep a fault in that bundle from becoming a church fire.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating the whole organ as one low-voltage system. The action circuits are capped at 30 volts dc by 650.4 — but the blower that feeds the wind is a line-voltage motor, wired and protected under Article 430 like any other motor.
inspection_fails: Legacy generator or replacement supply putting more than 30 volts dc on the action circuits (650.4).
26 AWG and 28 AWG action conductors protected at 20 amperes instead of not more than 6 amperes (650.8).
Action cables run in contact with 120-volt conductors inside the organ chamber (650.7).
Cotton- or enamel-insulated legacy wire reused instead of thermoplastic or thermosetting insulation (650.6(B)).
Rectifier case left unbonded from the equipment grounding conductor (650.5).

sections.title: Article 660 — X-Ray Equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 660 covers X-ray equipment — medical, dental, and industrial — and its field core is how the equipment is rated, disconnected, and fed.
• Two ratings run the article (660.2): the momentary rating is based on an operating interval of 5 seconds or less; the long-time rating on an interval of 5 minutes or longer.
• Disconnect (660.5): a disconnecting means in the supply circuit, rated at not less than 50 percent of the input required for the momentary rating or 100 percent of the input required for the long-time rating, whichever is greater — and operable from a location readily accessible from the X-ray control.
• Branch circuits (660.6(A)): conductor ampacity and overcurrent protection at not less than 50 percent of the momentary rating or 100 percent of the long-time rating, whichever is greater.
• Feeders (660.6(B)): a feeder supplying two or more X-ray branch circuits is figured at 100 percent of the momentary demand of the two largest units, plus 20 percent of the momentary ratings of the rest.
• Connection (660.4): fixed and stationary equipment is wired with a Chapter 3 method; equipment on a branch circuit of 30 A or less may be cord-and-plug connected.
• Healthcare work coordinates with Article 517, which carries parallel X-ray rules for health care facilities.
sections.on_the_job: Dental fit-out in Winter Park: the manufacturer's sheet for the panoramic unit gives a momentary rating of 100 A and a long-time rating of 20 A. The branch-circuit math is 50 percent of 100 A = 50 A against 100 percent of 20 A = 20 A — the bigger number governs, so the unit gets a 50 A branch circuit and a disconnect rated at least 50 A, mounted where the operator stands at the control. Sized off the 100 A headline alone, the circuit would be double what the Code asks; off the long-time rating alone, it would fail 660.6(A).
sections.why_it_exists: An X-ray tube draws its load in violent bursts — full power for a fraction of a second, then nothing. Sized like an ordinary load, the circuit is copper nobody needs; sized off the wrong rating, the breaker trips mid-exposure or conductors run hot during long fluoroscopy work. The two-rating system matches the wire to how the machine actually draws, and the disconnect by the control lets the operator kill the equipment from where it is run.
inspection_fails: Disconnect for the X-ray unit placed at the panel, out of reach of the operator's position at the control.
Branch circuit sized from the long-time rating only — 50 percent of the momentary rating was the greater number.
Feeder supplying two X-ray branch circuits sized with the branch-circuit 50 percent rule instead of 660.6(B).
Cord-and-plug connection used as the disconnect for equipment fed above 30 A.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing from the nameplate's biggest number — or from the small one. A unit marked 100 A momentary does not need a 100 A branch circuit: 660.6(A) asks for 50 percent of the momentary rating or 100 percent of the long-time rating, whichever is greater. Picking 100 percent of momentary oversizes; picking long-time alone undersizes. Run both numbers and take the greater.

sections.title: Article 665 — Induction and Dielectric Heating Equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 665 covers the construction and installation of induction heating, induction melting, induction welding and dielectric heating equipment and accessories for industrial and scientific applications (665.1). Medical and dental applications, appliances, and line-frequency pipeline and vessel heating sit outside it — pipeline heating lives in Article 427.
• Wiring from the source of power to the equipment follows Chapters 1 through 4 unless this article amends it (665.3).
• The equipment stays out of hazardous (classified) locations unless it and its wiring are approved for that location (665.4).
• The output circuit — everything external to the converting device — may be isolated from ground, and its current to ground is limited so that no 50 V or more to ground appears on any accessible part (665.5).
• Multiple control points are interlocked so the applicator can be energized from only one point at a time, with a way to de-energize at every point; foot switches get a shield against accidental closing (665.7).
• Supply conductor ampacity is built from the nameplate ratings of the largest group of equipment that can operate at the same time, plus the standby currents of the remaining equipment (665.10).
sections.on_the_job: Industrial only for Sharma: if a bid shows induction or dielectric heating, price only the supply disconnect and feeder shown on the engineered drawings. The disconnect belongs within sight of the equipment and capable of being locked in the open position (665.12). The equipment's shielding, guarding and interlocks are the manufacturer's listing — not field work, and not value-engineering targets. If the drawings don't show the supply, that is an RFI, not an allowance.

sections.why_it_exists: This equipment makes heat with high-frequency energy, and the output side does not behave like a branch circuit: RF voltage can appear on frames and nearby metal, capacitors hold a charge after shutdown, and an applicator energized from a second control point can start while a worker's hands are in it. The interlock, guarding and bonding rules exist because the hazard is invisible energy, not a sparking fault you can see coming.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating the output circuit like ordinary wiring that has to be grounded — 665.5 permits it isolated from ground, and grounding it 'to be safe' can defeat the design. The second trap is sizing the feeder by adding every nameplate on the floor: 665.10 counts the largest group that can run at once at full rating and the rest at standby current.
inspection_fails: Applicator can be energized from two control stations at once — control points not interlocked.
Foot switch with no shield over the contact button.
Feeder sized from Chapter 3 habits instead of the 665.10 nameplate method.
Equipment frames not bonded — RF voltage standing on exposed metal (665.26).

sections.title: Article 668 — Electrolytic Cells
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 668 covers electrolytic cells — the cell lines that make chlorine, caustic, aluminum and similar products by passing heavy DC current through a process. The recognition points:
• A cell line and its DC process power supply, inside the cell line working zone, are treated as one functional unit — a single line can run over 400,000 A DC at over 1000 V DC.
• Inside the zone, ordinary grounding logic is reversed on purpose. The DC process power supply conductors are not required to be grounded (668.11).
• Where that supply runs over 50 V between conductors, its metal enclosures are grounded through protective relaying or by a copper bonding conductor not smaller than 2/0 AWG (668.11).
• AC systems and exposed conductive surfaces inside the zone are not required to be grounded (668.30); the workers and their tools are insulated from ground instead.
• Any part of a crane or hoist that contacts an energized cell or its attachments must be insulated from ground (668.32).
• Each DC power supply to a cell line must be capable of being disconnected; a removable link in the busbar can be that disconnecting means (668.13).
• Outside the working zone, none of this applies — the rest of the NEC governs in full (668.3).
sections.on_the_job: Recognition only. If a scope ever shows a rectifier room, a cell line, or busbar runs feeding process tanks at a Florida chemical or plating plant, that is Article 668 territory — heavy industrial, and not Sharma work. Flag it to Sanjay and Mike the day it appears in a scope. If Sharma ever services ordinary building equipment in such a plant, that work sits outside the working zone and follows the normal rules — but nobody from a residential crew improvises inside the zone.
sections.why_it_exists: Cell line crews have to touch energized cell surfaces to run the process — the work cannot be done with everything dead and grounded. If the line, the tools and the crane were grounded the ordinary way, the worker would become the bridge between live parts and ground. So the article insulates the worker and the workplace from ground, and keeps the DC system floating, instead of insulating the conductor.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is the ordinary-practice answer: ground the DC conductors, ground the crane, ground the tools, and apply 110.26 working-space logic inside the zone. Inside the cell line working zone that is exactly backwards — 668.11 does not require the process conductors to be grounded, 668.32 requires crane parts contacting cells to be insulated from ground, and 668.3 keeps the ordinary articles for work outside the zone.
inspection_fails: Cell line treated as an ordinary grounded system — process conductors grounded against the 668.11 design.
Crane hook block contacting energized cells with no insulation from ground (668.32).
Portable tools in the zone fed from an ordinary grounded receptacle circuit instead of an isolated, ungrounded supply (668.20).
DC power supply with no means of being disconnected from its cell line (668.13).

sections.title: Article 669 — Electroplating
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 669 covers the electrical components and accessory equipment that supply power and controls for electroplating — and anodizing, electropolishing and electrostripping ride under the same rules; the Code calls all of it electroplating (669.1). This is industrial work: a rectifier feeds plating tanks at low voltage and very high current, often over bare busbar instead of ordinary branch-circuit wiring.
• Equipment must be identified for electroplating service (669.3).
• Branch-circuit conductors supplying the equipment need an ampacity of at least 125% of the total connected load (669.5).
• Busbars follow 366.23: bare copper busbar is capped at 1000 A per square inch of cross-section (669.5).
• At 60 V DC or less, insulated conductors may run without insulated supports if protected from physical damage, and bare copper or aluminum may run supported on insulators (669.6(A)).
• Over 60 V DC, insulated conductors need insulated supports, and bare conductors on insulators must be guarded against accidental contact up to the point of termination (669.6(B)).
• More than one power supply means a disconnecting means on the DC side of each supply (669.8(A)).
sections.on_the_job: Recognition only for Sharma. On an industrial bid for a plating shop, the rectifier nameplate and the plant engineer's busbar design drive everything. Say the connected load is 400 A of DC plating load: the branch circuit is sized at 500 A minimum (125%), and the bare copper busbar needs at least half a square inch of cross-section at the 1000 A per square inch cap — before voltage drop even enters the talk. Do not price plating-line conductors from Chapter 3 ampacity habits: the job needs the plant engineer's design before it needs an electrician.

sections.why_it_exists: A plating line is a burn and fire hazard wearing a low-voltage disguise. The volts sound harmless, but hundreds of amps through one loose busbar joint makes heat fast, and a DC arc does not self-extinguish at a zero crossing the way AC does. The 125% conductor rule, the busbar density cap and the guarding rules above 60 V exist because the failure mode is a glowing joint or an accidental touch in a wet, conductive chemical shop — not a tripped breaker.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing the supply like an ordinary Chapter 3 branch circuit — conductor ampacity equal to the load, or busbar picked by eye. 669.5 demands 125% of the total connected load, and busbar is capped by current density under 366.23, not by a Table 310.16 lookup. The other wrong answer is 'it is only 48 volts, so it is harmless' — at plating currents, low voltage is exactly where the burn hazard lives.
inspection_fails: Busbar joint discolored and hot — the run was pushed past the 1000 A per square inch density cap.
Branch circuit sized at 100% of the rectifier load — the 125% factor of 669.5 never applied.
Bare busbar over 60 V DC run where a worker can brush against it — no guarding to the termination.
Two rectifiers feeding one line, one disconnect — no DC-side disconnect for the second supply.

sections.title: Article 670 — Industrial Machinery
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 670 covers industrial machinery — machines with combined motor and control loads fed by one supply circuit. The machine's nameplate does the math: 670.3(A) requires the nameplate to supply the full-load current, the short-circuit current rating, and the largest-motor data, and 670.4(A) sets the supply-conductor ampacity:
• Not less than 125% of the full-load current of all resistance heating loads, plus
• 125% of the full-load current of the highest-rated motor, plus
• The full-load currents of all other motors and apparatus that can run at the same time, based on duty cycle
Use the supply-conductor ampacity the machine's nameplate or documentation states per 670.4(A) — not a 430 calculation run on the machine's internal motors.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: a machine whose nameplate gives a supply-circuit rating of 46 A is fed with conductors of at least that ampacity — use the supply-conductor ampacity the machine's nameplate/documentation states per 670.4(A) — not by opening the machine and adding its internal motors under 430. Photograph the nameplate for the takeoff; it is the calculation. Run the formula on a packaging machine in Kissimmee: resistance heat 16 A × 125% = 20 A, largest motor 24 A × 125% = 30 A, two auxiliaries at 6 A each = 12 A — the supply needs at least 62 A of ampacity before the breaker is even discussed.

nec2023_change.change: Revised Section 670.1 to now include overvoltage protection for supply conductors for industrial machinery.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 670.1 Scope. (Industrial Machinery)

sections.why_it_exists: A machine is not a motor. Inside one cabinet, heaters, the main drive, and auxiliaries cycle together in combinations the installer cannot see from outside. Sizing the supply from the nameplate formula keeps the feeder matched to the worst combination the manufacturer designed for — undersize it and the supply runs hot on a normal production cycle; open the machine and guess under 430 and the numbers are fiction.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is opening the machine and adding up its motors under Article 430. Article 670 forbids the detour: the nameplate and the 670.4(A) formula — 125% of the heat, 125% of the largest motor, 100% of everything else that can run together — set the supply ampacity.

tables.caption: 670.4(A) supply ampacity
tables.note: The nameplate per 670.3(A) supplies the currents: full-load current, SCCR, largest motor.

inspection_fails: Supply sized from a 430 motor calculation instead of the machine nameplate (670.4(A)).
Conductors smaller than the supply-conductor ampacity the nameplate states.
Nameplate data never recorded for the takeoff — the SCCR and largest-motor data never reached the job file.
Machine SCCR lower than the available fault current at its supply point.

page_quiz.question: Supply-conductor ampacity for an industrial machine is set by:

page_quiz.explain_plain: 670.4(A) builds the ampacity from the nameplate: 125% of heat, 125% of the largest motor, plus the rest that can run together.

page_quiz.question: Resistance heat 20 A, largest motor 20 A, other loads 10 A. Minimum supply ampacity?
The machine nameplate must supply all of these EXCEPT:
page_quiz.explain_plain: 670.3(A) nameplate data is electrical: full-load current, short-circuit current rating, and the largest motor.

sections.title: Article 675 — Electrically Driven or Controlled Irrigation Machines
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 675 covers electrically driven or controlled irrigation machines that are not portable by hand — center pivots, linear-move machines, and similar farm equipment. It does not cover the pumps that bring water to the machine. The parts a Sharma crew actually touches:
• 675.8 — the machine needs a main disconnecting means with overcurrent protection, at the point where power connects to the machine, or in view of the machine and not more than 50 ft away, readily accessible and capable of being locked in the open position.
• 675.11 — collector rings at the pivot carry power and control across the rotating joint. The rings are sized for the loads they carry, and the grounding ring is sized to the same rating as the power rings.
• 675.12 — all electrical equipment and enclosures on the machine are grounded, with the grounding path run to every motor and control on the spans.
• The irrigation cable interconnecting enclosures on the machine is an armored cable built for wet, flexing service, supported at least every 4 ft.
sections.why_it_exists: A center pivot is hundreds of feet of steel pipe and motors standing in a wet field, and it can start moving on a timer or a remote command while someone is working on a span. Workers have been hurt by pivots that started on their own, and by machine frames made live by a fault with no ground path back. The lockable disconnect and the full grounding are what make the machine safe to touch.
sections.on_the_job: Service call on a center pivot outside Ocala: before anyone touches the collector rings or the span wiring, the crew opens the machine disconnect at the pivot point, locks it, and tags it — the farm's controls can start a pivot remotely, so “the panel said off” is not enough. Then the checks: the disconnect sits in view of the machine and inside the 50 ft limit, the grounding conductor runs unbroken out the spans, and the grounding ring at the pivot is intact. The usual Florida finds are lightning damage at the pivot and a ground conductor cut at a span box.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer puts the main disconnect “anywhere on the farm panel.” 675.8(B) is specific: at the point of connection, or visible from the machine and not more than 50 ft away — with overcurrent protection included, and it must lock open. Second trap: the article does not cover the well pump that feeds the pivot; the pump is ordinary motor work under Article 430.

Grounding conductor cut at a span junction box, leaving the far spans floating.
Collector-ring enclosure open to the weather, with the grounding ring undersized.
Ordinary cord substituted for armored irrigation cable along the span.

page_quiz.explain_plain: 675.11 sizes the grounding ring fully, to the same rating as the power rings it serves with.

choices: The pumps that bring water to the machines
page_quiz.explain_plain: The scope stops at the machine itself; supply pumps fall under the general motor rules.

sections.title: Article 680 — Swimming Pools, Fountains, and Similar Installations
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 680 covers swimming pools, fountains, and similar installations, organized by installation type. The first job on any pool job is knowing which part you are in:
• Part I — general rules that ride with every part
• Part II — permanently installed pools
• Part III — storable pools
• Part IV — spas and hot tubs
• Part V — fountains
• Part VII — hydromassage bathtubs
• Part VIII — pool lifts
Two systems run through all of it and must never be confused. Grounding is the fault path back to the source. Equipotential bonding under 680.26 ties everything a swimmer can touch — the water, the deck, the pump — to one potential, and it never has to run back to a panelboard or a grounding electrode. Distances are measured the way a cord would travel: the required receptacle for a permanently installed pool sits not less than 6 ft and not more than 20 ft from the inside wall, and not more than 6 ft 6 in. above the deck or grade (680.22(A)). A junction box for an underwater light sits at least 4 ft from the inside wall and at least 4 in. above the deck, or 8 in. above the maximum water level, whichever is higher (680.24(A)). Florida is pool country — this is the highest-value article in the chapter for Sharma.
sections.on_the_job: Classify the install before pricing: a storable pool, an outdoor spa, and a permanently installed pool carry three different rule sets out of the same article. On a new Orlando backyard pool, Sharma's rough-in starts with the tape: the required receptacle lands in the 6–20 ft band from the inside wall, the deck box sits 4 ft out, 8 in. above the maximum water level, and the bonding grid ties shell steel, deck, and pump pad together before the pour. Miss the classification or the bonding and the fix is a saw cut, not a change order.
sections.figure_idea: Pool cross-section with callouts: receptacle band 6–20 ft, bonding ring under the deck, deck box at 4 ft, overhead clearance arrows.
sections.florida_note: Florida enforces NEC 2020 through the Florida Building Code 8th Edition (2023), for permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026; the FBC 9th Edition (2026) adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026. The NEC 2023 changes in this article apply in Florida to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026 (FBC 9th Ed.); earlier permits stay on NEC 2020.

sections.why_it_exists: Water, bare skin, and bare feet make the body a good conductor, and a swimmer cannot let go of a fault. A few volts between the water and the deck can paralyze a swimmer's muscles and drown them — electric shock drowning often leaves no mark. Bonding holds everything the swimmer can touch at one potential, GFCI protection cuts the fault off, and the distance rules keep receptacles and cords out of the splash zone.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating bonding as grounding. Running the grid back to the panel, or offering an EGC as a substitute for the 680.26 grid, both miss the rule: bonding ties everything the swimmer can touch to one potential, it is not required to extend to a panelboard, a service disconnect, or an electrode — and it never replaces the EGC in the branch circuit.

sections.title: Overhead conductor clearances
sections.plain_explanation:
In the 2020 edition the overhead rules live at 680.9(A) with Table 680.9(A) — older sources that cite 680.8 are working from a previous edition.
• The clearance in any direction from the water level, the edge of a diving structure, or the base of a diving platform is 22.5 ft for the conductors the table covers.
• Measured from maximum water level, the clearance to an observation stand, tower, or diving platform is 14.5 ft.
• All clearances are measured from maximum water level, not from the deck.
• Read Table 680.9(A) by its rows: the figures apply to the conductor types and voltages the table lists, measured as the table directs — they are not a blanket clearance for every wire over water.
• Overhead communications conductors and cables have their own rule at 680.9(B): a horizontal clearance of at least 10 ft from the pool and its associated structures.
sections.on_the_job: Survey the overhead lines before the pool layout is final — moving a pool shell is cheaper than relocating a service drop, and 22.5 ft in ANY direction includes diagonals. On a Lakeland backyard pool the utility drop crossed the deep-end corner: measured from maximum water level along the diagonal over the diving board it came in under 22.5 ft, so the pool shifted on the lot and the board moved to the shallow end before the shell was set.
sections.figure_idea: Elevation sketch: pool, diving board, and an overhead line with the 22.5 ft diagonal arrow.

sections.why_it_exists: Around a pool, people dive, stand on towers, and carry long metal poles upright — vacuum poles, skimmers, even sailboat masts on a marina job. A wire that looks high enough from the deck can sit inside the arc of a diver or the reach of a pole. Measuring from maximum water level, in every direction, keeps the conductor outside the space a person and a long object can occupy.
inspection_fails: Overhead conductor inside 22.5 ft of the water or a diving structure, measured in any direction (Table 680.9(A)).
Clearance measured from the deck instead of from maximum water level.
Observation stand, tower or diving platform inside 14.5 ft of an overhead conductor.
Communications cable over the pool or within 10 ft horizontally (680.9(B)).
Permit set citing 680.8 — previous-edition numbering; the 2020 rules are at 680.9.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is measuring 22.5 ft straight up from the water and calling it done. The table clearance runs in any direction — a conductor well above the water can still fail on the diagonal from the edge of a diving board. The second trap is the citation: 680.8 is a previous edition; the 2020 overhead rules are at 680.9.

sections.title: Underground wiring
sections.plain_explanation:
Underground wiring is not permitted under a pool, or within 5 ft horizontally of the inside wall of the pool, unless it is necessary to supply pool equipment permitted by this article. That one sentence decides most pool-deck trenching before it starts.
• Wiring that does run in the 5 ft zone uses the article's methods: rigid metal conduit, intermediate metal conduit, rigid polyvinyl chloride conduit, reinforced thermosetting resin conduit, or Type MC cable, suitable for the conditions at that location.
• Minimum cover for those runs comes from Table 300.5 — in general locations, 6 in. for rigid and intermediate metal conduit and 18 in. for rigid PVC and RTRC.
• Equipment grounding for anything in the zone follows the pool rules of this article, not the general rules alone.
• When in doubt, route around the 5 ft band. A longer trench outside the band is almost always cheaper than a failed inspection inside it.
sections.on_the_job: On a Winter Park pool job, the equipment pad sits 4 ft from the water's edge, so the pump and heater feeds cross the band: they run in rigid PVC at 18 in. of cover, the minimum Table 300.5 asks of PVC in a general location. The site-lighting conduit for the back fence tells the other half of the story — it does not serve the pool, so it stays outside the 5 ft band even though cutting the corner would save 30 ft of trench. Keep site lighting and landscape conduits out of the band unless they serve the pool itself.
sections.figure_idea: Plan view: pool shell with the 5 ft underground-wiring band shaded.

nec2023_change.change: Underground runs within 5 ft of a pool's inside wall now count as suitable only when the wiring method is installed as a complete system, from one outlet, junction or splice point to the next. The underground methods for the zone within 5 ft horizontally of the inside wall now count only when installed as complete systems (680.11(A)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 680.11 Underground wiring near pools

sections.why_it_exists: Water, bare feet, and a faulted buried conductor are a bad mix: a damaged cable under a deck can put voltage into the water and the wet concrete around it, and a swimmer has no way to let go or step away. Keeping foreign wiring out of the band — and the wiring that must cross it inside a tough raceway, buried deep — keeps pool faults on pool equipment, where the bonding and GFCI rules can manage them.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is "any conduit, buried deep, is fine in the band." Depth is only half the rule — the method list in 680.11 is closed, and under the pool itself the answer is simpler: nothing runs there except what the pool equipment needs.
inspection_fails: Direct-buried UF cable crossing the 5 ft band to feed landscape lighting.
Conduit run under the pool shell as a shortcut to the equipment pad.
Rigid PVC in the band buried with only a few inches of cover instead of the Table 300.5 minimum.
Site-lighting or irrigation wiring threaded through the band when a route outside it existed.

sections.title: Motor wiring and equipment grounding conductor
sections.plain_explanation:
Pool motor circuits carry an equipment grounding conductor with two pool differences from ordinary motor work:
• The EGC is insulated copper — not a bare conductor in the raceway, and not aluminum.
• It is sized from Table 250.122 by the overcurrent device ahead of the circuit — but never smaller than 12 AWG, even where the table would allow smaller.
The one place the floor bites: a 15 A circuit, where Table 250.122 pairs the breaker with a 14 AWG copper EGC. On a pool motor circuit that 14 AWG stays in the truck — the EGC is 12 AWG. At 20 A the table and the floor agree on 12 AWG; at 30 A and above the table takes over (10 AWG at 30, 40 and 60 A).
sections.on_the_job: Florida pool pad, new build: the pump motor is fed from a 20 A GFCI breaker (680.21(C)) in the Siemens panel. The crew pulls two circuit conductors and a green insulated 12 AWG copper EGC in the raceway to the motor — the table size for 20 A and the 680.21(A) floor are the same number here. On the same pad, a 15 A circuit for a small auxiliary pump still gets a 12 AWG insulated EGC, not the 14 AWG the table alone would allow.
sections.figure_idea: Equipment pad raceway opened: insulated green EGC alongside the circuit conductors.
sections.why_it_exists: The equipment pad is wet, outdoors, and tied into the pool's equipotential bonding. A bare ground wire in a damp raceway corrodes quietly for years, and the first anyone knows is when a fault has no path back and the breaker never trips — with swimmers in the water. The insulated copper conductor, held to a 12 AWG floor, keeps the fault path intact so the overcurrent device opens fast.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing the pool EGC straight off Table 250.122 and stopping there: 14 AWG for a 15 A circuit is the table's answer for ordinary work, and it is the wrong answer at a pool. 680.21(A) sets a floor of 12 AWG and requires the conductor to be insulated copper — a bare ground pulled in the conduit fails even at the right size.
inspection_fails: Bare equipment grounding conductor in the pool motor raceway — 680.21(A) requires it insulated.
14 AWG EGC on a 15 A pool motor circuit — below the 12 AWG floor.
Aluminum EGC on a pool motor circuit — the section requires copper.
EGC sized by the conductor size instead of by the overcurrent device ahead of it (Table 250.122).

tables.caption: Table 250.122 size vs the pool floor (copper EGC)
tables.note: The 12 AWG floor in 680.21(A) only changes the answer at 15 A; above that, the table governs.

figures.alt: Raceway run from a panel with a 20 A GFCI breaker to a pool pump motor, showing two circuit conductors and a green insulated equipment grounding conductor, a gold band stating the 12 AWG minimum, and a red panel showing a bare EGC as a fail.
figures.caption: Insulated copper EGC with the circuit — 12 AWG minimum, whatever the breaker.

page_quiz.question: Smallest EGC allowed on a pool motor circuit?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 680.21(A) sets the floor at 12 AWG even where Table 250.122 would allow 14 AWG.

page_quiz.question: The pool motor EGC must be:
page_quiz.explain_plain: Insulated copper is the pool difference — a bare conductor in the raceway does not comply.

page_quiz.question: EGC for a pool pump motor on a 40 A breaker?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Table 250.122 pairs a 40 A overcurrent device with a 10 AWG copper EGC, which is above the 12 AWG floor.

sections.title: GFCI protection for pool motors — re-checked
sections.plain_explanation:
GFCI protection is required for outlets supplying pool motors on branch circuits rated 150 volts or less to ground and 60 amperes or less, single-phase or three-phase.
• The protection covers the outlet — by receptacle or by direct connection. A hardwired pump is inside the rule, not outside it.
• The scope is all pool motors inside those ratings, not just cord-and-plug pumps. This page was re-checked against 2020-based sources before the chapter was written, and the v1 lookup (L-088) states the scope the same way.
• The motor circuit still needs its insulated copper equipment grounding conductor under 680.21(A), sized from Table 250.122 and never smaller than 12 AWG.
The protection device is planned at design and chosen for the job — see the Sharma note below.
sections.on_the_job: A hardwired 240V pool pump needs GFCI protection just as much as a plug-in one — plan the protection device at design, not at the final walk. On a Florida pool-equipment job, a 240-volt, 20-ampere pump circuit gets its GFCI protection arranged at the panel, the insulated copper equipment grounding conductor is 12 AWG minimum, and the protection is tested with the pump running before the final. Finding out at the final walk that the circuit is unprotected means a return trip and a failed inspection.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma note: like 625.54, a 240V pool circuit is not an S-07 120V DFN point. Meet 680.21(C) with the listed method specified for the job; device choice is Mike/Sanjay's per job.
sections.figure_idea: Pump circuit showing GFCI protection device ahead of a hardwired motor.

nec2023_change.change: Repairing a pool pump motor now triggers ground-fault protection, just like replacing one. The device matches the circuit: a GFCI, or a special purpose GFCI (SPGFCI) above 150 volts to ground. Repair now counts: a pump motor covered by 680.21(C) that's repaired, not only one that's replaced, needs ground-fault protection on its circuit (680.21(D)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 680.21 Repaired pool pump motors

sections.why_it_exists: A pool motor works within reach of the water, bonded into a system swimmers touch. A ground fault in a pump winding can put voltage on the equipment pad and into the water instead of tripping anything. GFCI protection watches for that leakage current and opens the circuit in milliseconds, before the fault becomes a shock in the pool.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that only cord-and-plug pool pumps need GFCI protection — the word 'outlet' fools people into picturing a receptacle. 680.21(C) covers outlets supplying pool motors by receptacle or by direct connection, so the hardwired 240-volt pump is covered. The second trap is stretching the scope: above 150 volts to ground or above 60 amperes, this subsection ends — check which rule applies instead of stretching this one.

tables.caption: 680.21(C) scope — is the outlet covered?
rows: Motor circuit over 150V to ground or 60A

inspection_fails: Hardwired 240V pump on a standard breaker — no GFCI protection on the outlet (680.21(C)).
Protection arranged for a receptacle that is not there — the direct-connected outlet left unprotected.
Pool motor equipment grounding conductor smaller than 12 AWG, or bare in the raceway (680.21(A)).
Replacement pump motor left running on the old unprotected circuit (680.21(D)).

page_quiz.question: Which pool motor outlet requires GFCI protection under 680.21(C)?
choices: A hardwired 240V pump on a 20A circuit
Only pumps with a receptacle in the equipment pad
page_quiz.explain_plain: The rule covers outlets by receptacle or by direct connection, on circuits rated 150V or less to ground and 60A or less — a hardwired 240V pump is covered.

page_quiz.question: The two scope limits in 680.21(C) are:
page_quiz.explain_plain: Branch circuits rated 150 volts or less to ground and 60 amperes or less, single-phase or three-phase.

page_quiz.explain_plain: The replacement duty rides with the motor change — an old unprotected circuit is not grandfathered once the motor is replaced.

sections.title: Replacement pump motors
sections.plain_explanation:
680.21(D) is a service rule: where a pool pump motor is replaced, the replacement work must provide the GFCI protection 680.21(C) requires for that outlet. A service call that swaps a motor on an old unprotected circuit does not get to leave it unprotected.
• The duty rides with the replacement, not with the age of the pool — an existing unprotected circuit is not grandfathered once the motor is changed.
• The (C) scope it points back to: outlets supplying pool motors on branch circuits rated 150 V or less to ground and 60 A or less, single-phase or three-phase, by receptacle or by direct connection.
sections.on_the_job: Service crews: a motor swap triggers the GFCI upgrade — quote it with the replacement, not as a surprise. A typical Florida call is a 240 V, 20 A hard-wired pump on a plain breaker: the replacement price carries the GFCI protection up front, and the tech verifies protection at the outlet before the new motor is left running — not after the callback.

nec2023_change.change: The revisions at 680.21(D) expand the requirement to provide ground- fault circuit-interrupter (GFCI) protection for replaced pool pump motors and also include those that are repaired, but not replaced.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 680.21{D) Pool Pump Motor Replacement

sections.why_it_exists: Pump motors live wet, tied into the same circulation system the swimmers touch. A motor swapped onto an unprotected circuit keeps the old shock hazard alive under a new motor's invoice. Tying the GFCI upgrade to the replacement closes the grandfather gap: at the one moment a qualified person is already standing at the equipment, the protection goes in.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is 'we only changed the motor — we never touched the circuit.' 680.21(D) makes the replacement itself the trigger, so the job fails if the outlet is left without the 680.21(C) GFCI protection, even though the wiring predates the rule. And read the edition note before quoting future work: under the 2023 change, a repair triggers the same duty.
inspection_fails: Motor replaced and the circuit left on a plain breaker — no GFCI protection at the outlet.
Quote written for the motor only; the GFCI upgrade sprung on the customer after the swap.
Replacement motor cord-connected to a receptacle that is not the protected outlet 680.21(C) requires.

page_quiz.explain_plain: In 2020, (D) is triggered by replacement. The 2023 change extends it to repaired motors — see the edition note.

sections.title: Receptacles — the 2020 lettering
sections.plain_explanation:
680.22(A) is where receptacles at a permanently installed pool live in the 2020 book. The lettering below was re-checked against 2020 before writing — older sources print different letters for the same rules, so cite the 2020 letters.
• (A)(1) The required receptacle — not less than 6 ft and not more than 20 ft from the inside wall of the pool, and not more than 6 ft 6 in. above the floor, platform, or grade serving the pool
• (A)(2) Receptacles serving pool circulation and sanitation equipment — not less than 6 ft away, grounding type, GFCI protected
• (A)(3) All other receptacles — not less than 6 ft from the inside wall
• (A)(4) GFCI protection — for all 125V, single-phase, 15A and 20A receptacles located within 20 ft of the inside wall
• (A)(5) A pool equipment room — at least one 125V, 15A or 20A receptacle, and GFCI protection for receptacles in the room
• (A)(6) How distances are measured — the shortest path a supply cord would follow, without passing through a floor, wall, ceiling, doorway, window, or other effective barrier
sections.on_the_job: Lay out the required receptacle in the 6–20 ft band at rough-in, before the deck and the screen enclosure fix every measurement. On a lanai pool, set the required receptacle on the house wall inside the band and under the 6 ft 6 in. height cap, and put the sanitation equipment receptacle at least 6 ft out with GFCI protection. Remember the tape follows the cord path: a receptacle that measures 8 ft in a straight line through the screen wall can measure much longer once the cord has to run around through the screen door — long enough to push it out of the band.
sections.figure_idea: Plan view: 6 ft inner line, 20 ft outer line, required receptacle between them; cord-path measurement around a barrier.
sections.florida_note: Florida enforces NEC 2020 through the Florida Building Code 8th Edition (2023), for permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026; the FBC 9th Edition (2026) adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026. The NEC 2023 changes in this article apply in Florida to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026 (FBC 9th Ed.); earlier permits stay on NEC 2020.
sections.why_it_exists: The band is a compromise written around a wet body. Inside 6 ft, a cord-connected appliance can reach the water with someone in it. Past 20 ft, the required receptacle is too far away to be the one people actually use, so cords get stretched across the deck instead. GFCI protection covers the whole 20 ft zone because that is where wet hands and bare feet meet receptacles.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is measuring with a straight-line tape through the screen enclosure, or quoting the letters from an older edition's study guide. 680.22(A)(6) measures the shortest path the cord would actually follow, with no pass-through at walls, doors or windows — and the 2020 lettering is what the inspector is holding.
inspection_fails: Required receptacle 4 ft from the inside wall — inside the 6 ft minimum.
Required receptacle 24 ft out — past the 20 ft end of the band, so it doesn't count.
Receptacles inside 20 ft with no GFCI protection.
Distances taped straight-line through the screen wall instead of along the cord path.
Pool equipment room with no receptacle, or receptacles in the room without GFCI.

figures.alt: Plan view of a pool deck showing the inside wall of the pool, dashed 6 ft and 20 ft lines, the gold required-receptacle band with a receptacle in it, and a dashed cord path running around a screen wall through its door to the pump equipment.
figures.caption: The 6–20 ft band, measured the way the cord runs.

page_quiz.question: The required receptacle at a permanently installed pool must sit in which distance band?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Not less than 6 ft and not more than 20 ft from the inside wall, and not more than 6 ft 6 in. high.

page_quiz.question: Maximum height of the required receptacle above the floor or grade serving the pool?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 680.22(A)(1) caps the height at 6 ft 6 in.

page_quiz.question: How are the distances in 680.22(A) measured?
choices: The shortest path a supply cord would follow, without passing through barriers
Around the center of the deck
page_quiz.explain_plain: (A)(6): the shortest cord path, without passing through a floor, wall, ceiling, doorway, window or other effective barrier.

sections.title: Lighting and fans over and near the pool
sections.plain_explanation:
680.22(B) sets the heights for luminaires, lighting outlets and ceiling-suspended fans over a pool and in the band around it. Every height is measured from maximum water level — not from the deck.
• New work (B)(1): a new luminaire, lighting outlet or fan above the pool, or within 5 ft horizontally of the inside wall, must be at least 12 ft above maximum water level.
• Existing work (B)(3): an existing luminaire or fan in that same zone may stay where it is if it is at least 5 ft above the water, rigidly attached, and GFCI protected.
• The 5 to 10 ft band (B)(4): luminaires in the band from 5 to 10 ft horizontally need GFCI protection, unless they are at least 5 ft above the water and rigidly attached.
• Low voltage (B)(6): listed low-voltage luminaires have their own path through 680.23(A)(2).
sections.on_the_job: A lanai job in Winter Haven: the homeowner wants a new ceiling fan centered over the shallow end, under a roof that sits 10 ft 6 in above the water. That is new work inside the zone, so (B)(1) wants 12 ft — the fan cannot go there. It moves out past the 5 ft line, or the plan changes. The existing wall lantern beside the pool, 6 ft above the water and rigidly mounted, stays — once its circuit gets GFCI protection per (B)(3). Measure both from maximum water level; the deck tape lies to you by the depth of the pool wall.
sections.figure_idea: Elevation: new fixture at 12 ft over water; existing fixture grandfathered at 5 ft with GFCI.
sections.why_it_exists: A swimmer standing in the water is wet, barefoot and holding onto whatever is overhead. A fixture inside arm's reach puts line voltage one wet hand away from a person whose body is a good path to the water. Height is the protection: 12 ft puts new fixtures beyond reach and beyond the splash zone of a fixture that falls, and the GFCI and rigid-mount conditions are what let an older, lower fixture stay in service safely.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: '5 ft is the minimum height over a pool.' Five feet is the floor for existing fixtures that are rigidly attached and GFCI protected. A new fixture over the water or within 5 ft of the inside wall needs 12 ft above maximum water level. The second trap is measuring from the deck — every height on this page starts at maximum water level.
inspection_fails: New luminaire over the pool at 10 ft above the water — new work needs 12 ft (B)(1).
Heights measured from the deck instead of maximum water level.
Existing fixture kept at 5 ft with no GFCI protection, or hanging from a chain instead of rigidly attached.
Luminaire in the 5 to 10 ft band, under 5 ft above the water, with no GFCI protection (B)(4).
Ceiling fan installed over the water inside the 5 ft zone at lanai roof height.

figures.caption: Heights start at maximum water level — never at the deck.

page_quiz.question: A new luminaire goes directly over a pool. Minimum height above maximum water level?
page_quiz.explain_plain: New work over the water or within 5 ft of the inside wall: 12 ft minimum, (B)(1). The 5 ft figure is for existing fixtures only.

page_quiz.question: An existing fan hangs 6 ft above the water inside the zone. What lets it stay?

sections.title: Switching devices — 5 ft from the water
sections.plain_explanation:
Switching devices — the switches that control pool-area equipment and lighting — must be located at least 5 ft horizontally from the inside wall of the pool, spa, or hot tub, unless they are separated from the water by a permanent barrier, such as a solid wall or fence, that keeps a person in the water from reaching the switch.
• The measurement follows the same thinking as the receptacle rules in 680.22(A): distance is about what a wet hand can reach, not about where the device looks convenient on the plan.
• Switches that are part of a listed assembly, or that the article specifically permits closer in, are exceptions to read on the equipment itself — not a general permission.
sections.on_the_job: Florida pool with a screen enclosure: at rough-in, Sharma puts the pool light switch and the pump control on the house wall or the equipment pad, outside the 5 ft line — on this job the light switch landed 7 ft from the inside wall. The classic correction is the switch roughed in on the pool-side face of a screen-enclosure post, about 3 ft from the water, where a swimmer can touch it without leaving the pool. Moving it after the tile and deck are in costs ten times what the rough-in layout did.
sections.figure_idea: Plan view: 5 ft switching-device line around the water, barrier exception shown at a fence.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A person in the water is bonded to the water and surrounded by grounded, wet surfaces — about the best ground path a fault could ask for. A switch within reach invites that swimmer to run the pump or the lights with a wet hand, and any fault in the equipment then has a path through the swimmer's body. Five feet of distance — or a permanent barrier that does the same job — breaks the reach.
inspection_fails: Pool light switch roughed in on the pool-side face of a screen-enclosure post, inside the 5 ft line from the inside wall.
Pump and light controls at the equipment pad within reach of the water, with no permanent barrier between the switch and the pool.
Switching device measured from the deck edge and landing less than 5 ft from the inside wall of the pool.
Pool lighting timer inside the 5 ft zone on the pool wall, reachable by a person standing in the water.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is measuring from the wrong line. The 5 ft runs from the inside wall of the pool — not the deck edge, not the coping, not the outside face of the pool wall. Measured from the deck edge, a switch can look legal on the plan and still land within a wet reach of the water.

sections.title: Underwater luminaires
sections.plain_explanation:
Underwater luminaires must be listed for the purpose and installed by niche type — wet-niche, dry-niche, or no-niche — with transformers and power supplies for low-voltage units listed for pool use under 680.23(A)(2).
• Units operating above the low-voltage contact limit get GFCI protection.
• Wall-mounted units sit with the top of the lens at least 18 in. below the normal water level, unless the luminaire is listed and marked for use at a lesser depth.
The 'low-voltage contact limit' this section leans on is a defined term (680.2): not more than 15 V AC sinusoidal (RMS), 21.2 V peak for nonsinusoidal AC, or 30 V for continuous DC, with its own limits for interrupted DC. A listed low-voltage luminaire system at or under that limit is the path that avoids GFCI protection for the luminaire circuit; anything operating above the limit is GFCI protected. When a pool-light quote says 'low voltage,' confirm which side of that definition the system sits on before the protection is priced.
sections.on_the_job: The light, its niche, its transformer, and its junction box are one system — check all four against the listing. On an Orlando pool, the wall light mounts with the top of its lens 18 in. below normal water level and the transformer is listed for pool use; the system operates at or below the 680.2 contact limit, so the luminaire circuit takes the path the listing allows — confirmed from the luminaire's paperwork, not from the words 'low voltage' on the quote.
sections.figure_idea: Wet-niche luminaire cross-section with the 18 in. lens depth marked.

nec2023_change.change: Substantiation was received that rigid metal conduit extending directly to wet niche luminaires in forming shells of pools must be as listed red brass or listed stainless steel.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 680.23(B}(2}(a} Forming Shell. (Metal Conduit}

NEC 2023 CHANGE:

sections.why_it_exists: The fixture lives in the water swimmers touch, fed through the pool wall. If the luminaire, its niche and its supply are not one listed system, a fault can put the water itself at voltage. The 18 in depth keeps the lens submerged, cooled and out of easy reach, and the contact-limit line decides where GFCI protection has to stand behind the system.
inspection_fails: Wall luminaire with the top of the lens less than 18 in. below normal water level, and not listed and marked for the lesser depth.
Luminaire operating above the low-voltage contact limit with no GFCI protection.
Transformer or power supply for a low-voltage luminaire not listed for pool use (680.23(A)(2)).
Luminaire not listed for underwater use, or set in the wrong niche type.
'Low voltage' taken on faith — the system was never checked against the 680.2 contact limit (15 V RMS / 21.2 V peak / 30 V DC).
sections.exam_trap: The trap is hearing 'low voltage' and skipping GFCI without checking the definition. The contact limit is hard numbers in 680.2 — 15 V RMS sinusoidal, 21.2 V peak nonsinusoidal, 30 V continuous DC. A system above the limit is not low voltage for this section, whatever the quote called it, and it needs GFCI protection.

sections.title: Junction boxes for underwater luminaires
sections.plain_explanation:
A junction box tied to a conduit that runs directly to the forming shell of an underwater luminaire has to be a real pool box, in the right place:
• Listed, labeled, and identified as a swimming pool junction box.
• Located not less than 4 ft from the inside wall of the pool, unless separated by a solid fence, wall, or other permanent barrier.
• Set at an elevation of not less than 4 in. above the ground or pool deck, or not less than 8 in. above maximum water level — whichever gives the greater elevation.
• A flush deck box is permitted only for systems at or below the low-voltage contact limit — 15 V AC sinusoidal (RMS), 21.2 V peak for nonsinusoidal AC, or 30 V continuous DC, per the 680.2 definition — and it still sits at least 4 ft out.
sections.on_the_job: Pool at a Marion Oaks house: the finished deck will sit about 2 in. above the normal waterline. Four inches above that deck is only 6 in. above the water, so the 8 in. above maximum water level governs — set the box on its riser at that height, a full 4 ft back from the inside wall, and check both numbers with a tape and a level at rough-in, before the deck pour. "Close enough" fails on both numbers.
sections.figure_idea: Deck box elevation sketch — 8 in. above max water, 4 in. above deck, 4 ft from inside wall.
sections.why_it_exists: This box holds splices for a light that sits underwater, a few feet from people swimming. Height above the waterline keeps splash, surge, and deck wash-down out of the splices. Distance from the wall keeps the box out of the wettest zone at the pool edge and leaves room to service the conduit run. A generic box at deck level puts line-voltage splices where water stands.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer reads only one height: "4 in. above the deck" and stops. The rule takes whichever elevation is greater — 4 in. above ground or deck, or 8 in. above maximum water level. On a low deck, the water number controls. The second trap: a flush deck box is fine anywhere. It is permitted only at or below the low-voltage contact limit, and still 4 ft from the wall.
inspection_fails: Generic junction box installed instead of one listed and identified as a swimming pool junction box.
Box set 2 ft from the inside pool wall with no permanent barrier.
Box 4 in. above the deck but less than 8 in. above maximum water level on a low deck.
Flush deck box installed on a 120 V luminaire system above the low-voltage contact limit.

page_quiz.question: Minimum distance from the inside wall of the pool to a junction box for an underwater luminaire (no barrier)?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Not less than 4 ft from the inside wall, unless a solid fence, wall, or other permanent barrier separates it.

page_quiz.question: The box must sit at least how far above maximum water level?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 8 in. above maximum water level — or 4 in. above ground or deck, whichever gives the greater elevation.

page_quiz.question: When is a flush deck box permitted?
choices: Only where the system operates at or below the low-voltage contact limit, and still at least 4 ft out
page_quiz.explain_plain: Flush deck boxes are a low-voltage-contact-limit permission only; the 4 ft distance still applies.

sections.title: Feeders supplying pool equipment panelboards
sections.plain_explanation:
Where a feeder supplies a panelboard that serves pool, spa, or fountain equipment, 680.25 holds the feeder to a stricter standard than an ordinary feeder:
• The feeder is installed in one of the raceway wiring methods the section lists — not run as a cable assembly.
• It carries a copper equipment grounding conductor, sized from Table 250.122 with a minimum size set by the section, so the fault path is a wire conductor pulled with the feeder.
• The point is the same as in 680.21(A) for motors: around water, the fault path is a real wire conductor, not the raceway alone.
This page is not yet verified: the full wiring-method list, the minimum grounding-conductor size, and whether the 2020 text still requires that conductor to be insulated are held off this page until they are checked against the printed 2020 text — see the Check in print box.
sections.on_the_job: Feeding a pool subpanel from the house panel on a Marion County new build: the run goes in raceway the whole way, with a copper equipment grounding conductor pulled with the feeder and sized from Table 250.122. Before the pull, the foreman checks the printed 680.25 for the section's minimum size and its exact grounding-conductor wording — this page has not been verified against the 2020 text — and a feeder roughed in cable with no pulled ground is the correction waiting to happen.
sections.figure_idea: Feeder run from house panel to pool panelboard: raceway shown, insulated EGC called out at 12 AWG minimum.
sections.unverified_reason: Still unverified after Mike Holt recheck (2026-11-25): The wiring-method list looks incomplete: the page names only RMC, IMC, PVC or 'another identified raceway', but the code list also includes LFMC, LFNC, RTRC, EMT (on or within a building), ENT (within a building) and Type MC (within a building, not in a corrosive environment), plus an exception for existing feeders. I also could not confirm first-hand whether NEC 2020 still requires the feeder EGC to be INSULATED in 680.25(B) — the 2020 cycle changed several Article 680 grounding/wiring-method rules. Check 680.25(A) and (B) against the printed 2020 text, then publish the full list and the confirmed EGC wording. 'Table 250.122, not smaller than 12 AWG' is consistent with earlier editions.
sections.why_it_exists: A pool panelboard feeds pumps, lights and heaters that sit in or beside the water, often at the end of a long outdoor run. If that feeder's fault path is weak — a raceway joint corroded open, a ground that was never pulled — a fault at the equipment pad can sit energized indefinitely with swimmers a few feet away. 680.25 makes the feeder itself part of the protection: a raceway for physical protection, and a real copper grounding conductor sized from Table 250.122.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating the pool panel feeder like any other subpanel feeder: cable assembly, raceway optional, ground sized by habit. 680.25 is a stricter feeder rule — a raceway method from the section's list, a copper equipment grounding conductor, and Table 250.122 sizing. The second trap is quoting the minimum grounding-conductor size from memory: on this page, that number waits for the printed book.
inspection_fails: Pool panelboard feeder run in cable with no raceway — a 680.25 feeder uses one of the wiring methods the section lists.
No equipment grounding conductor pulled with the pool feeder — the raceway alone relied on as the fault path.
Feeder equipment grounding conductor sized by guess instead of from Table 250.122.

sections.title: Equipotential bonding — the idea
sections.plain_explanation:
Bonding is not grounding, and 680.26 is where the difference lives.
• What bonding does: it ties everything a swimmer can touch — the water, the deck, ladders, handrails, the pump — into one equipotential mass, so every touchable part sits at the same potential.
• Why it works: current through a person is driven by the voltage difference between two points the body bridges. Kill the difference and there is nothing to drive current, whatever the absolute voltage is.
• Where it stops: the bonding system is not required to extend back to a panelboard, a service disconnecting means, or a grounding electrode.
• What it never does: bonding never substitutes for the equipment grounding conductor in the branch circuit. The pool gets both systems, for two different hazards.
sections.on_the_job: Two systems, two purposes, and the crew that can say it passes pool inspections: the green equipment grounding conductor in the pump conduit carries fault current back to the panel so the breaker trips; the bare 8 AWG bonding grid around the shell kills voltage differences so nobody becomes a conductor. On a new pool in Ocala both run in the same trench — the green wire in the conduit to the pump, the bare 8 AWG ring around the shell tied to the steel, the ladder cups and the pump lug. Land either one in place of the other and the inspection fails.
sections.figure_idea: Swimmer touching a ladder and the water, both bonded to the same grid — no potential difference arrows.
sections.why_it_exists: Pool water and wet concrete pick up small voltage gradients from the earth, the utility neutral and nearby faults — a volt or two is common, and a swimmer's wet body is an excellent conductor. A person bridging two points at different potentials becomes the path. Equipotential bonding removes the gradient at the pool itself, so the water, the deck and the ladder are all one voltage and there is no path through the swimmer.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'bonding is just grounding by another name — run the grid back to the grounding electrode and you are done.' No. 680.26 does not require the bonding system to extend to a panelboard, a service disconnect or an electrode, and bonding never replaces the equipment grounding conductor. Grounding clears faults; bonding kills differences. The exam wants both, doing different jobs.
inspection_fails: No equipotential bonding grid installed — pool equipment 'grounded' with the green EGC only.
Metal ladder and handrail not bonded into the grid.
Bonding conductor connected to the pump but never tied to the pool reinforcing steel.
Bonding jumper landed on the grounding electrode and stopped — deck, water and equipment never tied together.
EGC omitted because 'the equipment is bonded' — bonding never substitutes for the EGC.

figures.alt: Plan view of a pool: a bare 8 AWG bonding ring around the shell ties the water, ladder and pump to one potential, while the green equipment grounding conductor runs separately from the pump back to the panel.
figures.caption: Bonding kills differences; the green wire clears faults.

page_quiz.question: What does equipotential bonding around a pool actually do?
choices: Carries fault current to the breaker
Ties touchable parts to one potential so no difference can drive current through a swimmer
Connects the pool to the grounding electrode
page_quiz.explain_plain: Bonding kills the voltage difference between the water, the deck and the equipment — it is the difference that drives current through a person.

page_quiz.question: The bonding system must extend back to which of these?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 680.26 does not require the bonding system to extend to a panelboard, a service disconnecting means, or a grounding electrode.

page_quiz.question: The pump is bonded with the 8 AWG grid. Is the green EGC in its conduit still required?
choices: Yes — bonding never substitutes for the EGC
page_quiz.explain_plain: Two systems, two hazards: bonding kills differences, the EGC clears faults. Both are required.

sections.title: Equipotential bonding — what gets bonded, and how
sections.plain_explanation:
The parts in 680.26(B)(1) through (B)(7) are bonded together with a solid copper conductor not smaller than 8 AWG, connected with a listed pressure connector, a terminal bar, or another listed means per 250.8(A):
• (B)(1) Conductive pool shells — the structural reinforcing steel, or the copper conductor grid that serves as the alternate where a conductive shell's steel is encapsulated in a nonconductive compound or is not available. A nonconductive shell (vinyl, fiberglass) is not a conductive shell at all and needs no shell bonding grid
• (B)(2) Perimeter surfaces — covered on the next page
• (B)(3) Metallic components
• (B)(4) Underwater lighting forming shells and mounting brackets
• (B)(5) Metal fittings larger than 4 in. that penetrate the shell
• (B)(6) Electrical equipment — with the (B)(6)(a) rule for double-insulated pump motors: the double-insulated motor itself is NOT bonded; instead an 8 AWG solid copper bonding conductor is provided at the grid so a future replacement motor that is not double-insulated can be bonded
• (B)(7) Fixed metal parts within 5 ft horizontally of the inside walls (with the vertical-separation exception at 12 ft)
sections.on_the_job: Walk the (B) list physically at rough-in — shell, steel, fittings, equipment, nearby metal — before anything is buried or shot. On a gunite pool, that means the shell steel and the perimeter steel before the pour, the light niches and every fitting over 4 in. as they are set, and the equipment pad before it is piped in. The double-insulated pump gets no bond wire on the motor — but the 8 AWG solid stub goes in at the grid anyway, coiled and labeled, because the replacement motor in ten years may not be double-insulated.
sections.figure_idea: Bonding grid plan with the seven (B) categories called out.
sections.why_it_exists: The grid is not there to clear faults — the equipment grounding conductor does that. It is there so everything a swimmer can touch at once sits at the same potential: shell steel, water, fittings, the pump, the fence. A voltage difference that would never trip a breaker can still drive current through a wet body between two “safe” pieces of metal. One grid, one potential.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer bonds the double-insulated pump motor itself — or skips the stub entirely because “this motor doesn't need one.” 680.26(B)(6)(a) is the opposite of both: the motor is NOT bonded, and the 8 AWG solid copper conductor is still provided at the grid, waiting for the future replacement motor that is not double-insulated.
inspection_fails: Bonding run in stranded conductor instead of the required 8 AWG solid copper.
Double-insulated pump motor bonded to the grid — or no 8 AWG stub left for its replacement.
Metal fitting over 4 in. penetrating the shell left off the grid.
Metal fence within 5 ft of the inside wall never bonded.
Bonding connections made with unlisted clamps instead of a 250.8 means.

sections.title: Perimeter surfaces — the ring
sections.plain_explanation:
The bonded perimeter surface reaches 3 ft beyond the inside walls of the pool — the deck a wet swimmer stands on has to sit at the same potential as the water.
• The ring method: one or more bare, solid copper conductors, not smaller than 8 AWG.
• Placement: laid 18 to 24 in. out from the inside walls of the pool, and 4 to 6 in. below the subgrade.
• Connections: attached to the pool's reinforcing steel or copper grid at a minimum of four uniformly spaced points.
Get the ring in before the deck — after pavers or a pour, neither the distance nor the depth can be checked or fixed.
sections.on_the_job: A new pool in Ocala, 16 by 32 ft: the ring goes in at rough — one bare 8 AWG solid copper conductor, taped off at 21 in. out from the inside walls and 5 in. below the subgrade, clamped to the shell steel at four points spread evenly around the pool. The inspector measures both numbers before the pavers arrive, because after the deck is down neither can be verified or repaired without demolition. That sequencing — ring first, deck second — is the whole job on this page.
sections.figure_idea: Section through the deck edge: ring at 18–24 in. out, 4–6 in. below subgrade, tie points marked.

nec2023_change.change: Perimeter bonding depth is now measured from finished grade: no deeper than 6 in under paving, 4 to 6 in under bare ground. An interim amendment later rewrote the perimeter rules again. As printed in 2023, a copper ring or grid goes in or under paving, no more than 6 in below finished grade (680.26(B)(2)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 680.26 Pool perimeter bonding

sections.why_it_exists: The swimmer steps out of the water onto the deck with wet feet, one hand still on a ladder or the water itself. If the deck surface sits at a different potential from the water, that step bridges the difference. Bonding the perimeter surface out to 3 ft puts the whole step-off zone at water potential, so there is no gradient under the swimmer's feet.
sections.exam_trap: Two traps. First: 'the ring can sit anywhere under the deck.' It has a window — 18 to 24 in. out, 4 to 6 in. below subgrade, four tie points minimum. Second: measuring the depth from finished grade. That is the 2023 change, in the edition box; the 2020 rule on this page measures 4 to 6 in. below the subgrade. Permits through Dec 30, 2026 stay on 2020.
inspection_fails: Ring buried outside the window — 30 in. out from the wall or 10 in. deep; the rule is 18–24 in. and 4–6 in. below subgrade.
Ring tied to the reinforcing steel at one point only — four uniformly spaced connections minimum.
Deck poured before the ring was inspected — depth and distance can no longer be verified.
Stranded or insulated conductor used for the ring — it must be bare solid copper, 8 AWG minimum.
Perimeter bonding stops at the coping — the bonded surface must reach 3 ft beyond the inside walls.
