sections.title: Pool water bonding — 9 square inches
sections.plain_explanation:
680.26 builds one equipotential bonding system around a pool, and (C) covers the hardest part of it: the pool water itself must be bonded.
• Where a bonded part — a ladder rail, a light niche, a metal fitting — is already in direct contact with the water, that contact does the job. No extra fitting is required.
• Where nothing bonded touches the water, an approved corrosion-resistant conductive surface of at least 9 sq in. must be in contact with it — the familiar listed water-bonding fitting in the skimmer or in the pump line.
• The fitting is not a stand-alone part: it ties back into the equipotential bonding system with the 680.26 bonding conductor, solid copper not smaller than 8 AWG.
• The math is simple: a 3 in. by 3 in. plate is exactly 9 sq in. Anything smaller does not comply.
sections.on_the_job: All-plastic pools with vinyl liners and no metal in the water are the trap — check for the 9 sq in. contact on every job. On a vinyl-liner pool in Ocala, the shell is plastic, the ladder is plastic, and the light is a plastic niche: nothing bonded touches the water. The fix is the listed water-bond fitting in the skimmer, its plate giving the full 9 sq in. of contact, tied back to the bonding grid with 8 AWG solid copper. Check it at the bonding inspection, while the fitting can still be reached — after the deck is poured and the pool is filled, nobody wants to drain it to prove a plate size.
sections.figure_idea: Skimmer with a listed water-bond plate, 9 sq in. dimensioned.
sections.why_it_exists: A swimmer is immersed in the water, holding the ladder, standing on the deck. If the water sits at a different voltage than the metal around it, the swimmer's body becomes the path between the two. Bonding the parts in 680.26(B) is not enough by itself — on an all-plastic pool, every listed part can be bonded and the water can still float at its own potential, because nothing bonded ever touches it. Paragraph (C) closes that last gap.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is answering that the pump motor's equipment grounding conductor bonds the water. It does not. 680.26(C) wants a bonded, corrosion-resistant conductive surface of at least 9 sq in. actually in contact with the water — or a bonded part that already touches it.
inspection_fails: All-plastic or vinyl-liner pool with no water-bond fitting — nothing bonded touches the water.
Water-bond plate with less than 9 sq in. of contact area in the water.
Fitting set in the skimmer but never tied into the equipotential bonding system.
Contact surface painted, scaled, or corroded — no longer conductive contact with the water.

sections.title: Storable pools — Parts I and III only
sections.plain_explanation:
A storable pool — and a storable spa or hot tub — is governed by Parts I and III of Article 680, and 680.26 equipotential bonding does not apply to it.
• The pump and equipment rules of Part III substitute for the Part II regime.
• Classification is the whole game: the same backyard water is a different code job depending on whether the pool is storable or permanently installed.
• 'Storable' is a defined term, not a synonym for above-ground: under 680.2, a storable pool is one built to be stored away, with a maximum water depth of 42 in. and walls of nonmetallic molded polymeric construction or inflatable fabric.
• A permanently installed above-ground pool does not meet that definition — it is Part II work, bonding included.
sections.on_the_job: A homeowner in Kissimmee has an inflatable-wall pool with 42 in. of water that comes down every fall — storable: Parts I and III, no 680.26 bonding grid. The house next door has a steel-wall above-ground pool that stays up year-round on a slab — permanently installed: Part II work, bonding included. Same street, same water, two different code jobs. Confirm which one it is before the quote, not at the inspection.
sections.why_it_exists: The two regimes protect people differently. A permanent pool sits in place for years with hard-wired equipment around wet bathers, so Part II wraps it in equipotential bonding and the full pump rules. A storable pool is seasonal equipment that is set up, used and put away. Bond a storable pool like a gunite pool and the work is wasted; wire a permanent pool like a storable one and swimmers lose the bonding protection the Code requires.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'above-ground means storable.' It does not. The 680.2 definition controls: built to be stored away, 42 in. maximum water depth, nonmetallic molded polymeric or inflatable fabric walls. A steel-wall pool that stays up is permanently installed even though it sits above ground — and it gets Part II, bonding included.
inspection_fails: Permanently installed above-ground pool wired under Part III — no 680.26 equipotential bonding installed.
Pool permitted as storable with a water depth over the 42 in. limit in the 680.2 definition.
Metal-wall pool classified as storable — the definition requires nonmetallic molded polymeric or inflatable fabric walls.

sections.title: Spas and hot tubs — Parts I and IV (outdoor adds Part II)
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 680 sorts its water by what the installation is, and spas and hot tubs land in Part IV.
• Part I (general rules) rides with every spa and hot tub.
• Part IV is the part written for spas and hot tubs.
• An outdoor spa or hot tub also picks up the Part II rules that Part IV points to through 680.42 — receptacle distances, GFCI protection, and equipotential bonding arrive through that door.
• An indoor spa follows Parts I and IV; the 680.42 door to Part II is written for outdoor installations.
• A self-contained factory spa package still lands on an installation that must meet the article. The listing covers the tub as built; it does not waive the field wiring rules.
sections.on_the_job: Outdoor spa on a lanai in Orlando: the tub arrives as one factory box, but the job is still a Part II checklist — receptacle distances and GFCI protection checked before trim, the equipotential bonding run in solid copper, 8 AWG minimum, and the pump circuit's equipment grounding conductor insulated copper, never smaller than 12 AWG. An indoor spa in a sunroom the following week gets Parts I and IV only: the same care with the circuit and its protection, but the 680.42 door to Part II stays closed.
sections.why_it_exists: A spa puts a bather's whole body in warm, moving water, in direct contact with jets, lights, and metal fittings. Wet skin and full contact drop body resistance, so a small fault that would only tingle on dry skin can drive dangerous current through a person in the tub. The layered parts exist so the protection written for pools follows the same water when it shows up in a smaller vessel outdoors.
inspection_fails: Outdoor spa wired as a plain appliance circuit — no bonding conductor run to the tub's bonding lug.
Receptacle inside the Part II distance limits because 'the tub is only a spa, not a pool.'
GFCI protection omitted on the spa circuit — the factory listing was treated as covering the field wiring.
Pump equipment grounding conductor run bare, or in 14 AWG; 680.21(A) wants insulated copper, 12 AWG minimum.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating the factory package as a finished installation: 'It is listed and self-contained, so we just set it and plug it in.' The listing covers the equipment as manufactured. It does not cover the branch circuit, the receptacle location, GFCI protection, or bonding in the field — outdoors, those arrive through 680.42's reference into Part II, and skipping them is the fail.

sections.title: Spa emergency shutoff — 5 ft, in sight, labeled
sections.plain_explanation:
Spas and hot tubs anywhere other than one-family dwellings must have an emergency shutoff for the recirculation and jet system.
• Readily accessible — a bystander can get to it without climbing, moving obstacles, or opening a locked gate.
• Adjacent to and within sight of the tub — the person using it can see the water it protects.
• At least 5 ft away from the tub — close enough to reach fast, far enough that a person in the water cannot touch it.
• Clearly labeled as the emergency shutoff.
sections.on_the_job: Amenity-center spa at a Kissimmee condo project: the recirculation and jet pumps get an emergency shutoff on the wall facing the tub, 8 ft from the inside wall — past the 5 ft minimum — in plain sight of anyone standing at the water, with a label that reads EMERGENCY SHUTOFF. The inspector paced the distance and read the label from the deck. The same tub model installed at a single-family home the next month needs no 680.41 shutoff at all — the section does not reach one-family dwellings — so the crew's first question on any spa job is which occupancy they are in.
sections.figure_idea: Amenity-center spa with the labeled shutoff on the wall 5 ft away, in sight.

nec2023_change.change: Spas and hot tubs get an equipment setback in new 680.41(B): gear above the low-voltage contact limit needs 5 ft of horizontal distance from the inside wall unless a permanent barrier stands between. Anything above the low-voltage contact limit stays 5 ft or more, measured horizontally, from the inside wall of the spa or hot tub (680.41(B)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 680.41 Spa equipment setback

sections.why_it_exists: Entrapment and medical emergencies in a spa are measured in seconds: hair or a limb caught on a suction fitting, a bather in distress with the jets driving the water. The shutoff has to be findable by a stranger — a hotel guest, a lifeguard, a parent — without instructions. The 5 ft floor keeps the person in trouble from being the only one who can reach it, and the label removes the guessing about which switch on the wall it is.
inspection_fails: Emergency shutoff mounted 3 ft from the tub's inside wall — inside the 5 ft minimum.
Shutoff present but unlabeled, one of four identical switches on the amenity wall.
Hotel spa with no emergency shutoff at all — the crew applied the one-family dwelling carve-out to an amenity installation.
Shutoff behind the locked equipment gate: not readily accessible, and not within sight of the tub.
sections.exam_trap: Two traps share this section. The first: mounting the shutoff within arm's reach of the water 'so it is handy' — inside 5 ft it fails, because a person in the tub must not be able to reach it. The second: skipping the shutoff at a hotel or condo spa because the backyard version did not need one — the one-family dwelling carve-out does not travel to amenity work.

sections.title: Outdoor spas and hot tubs — Part II rides along (680.42)
sections.plain_explanation:
An outdoor spa or hot tub is not Part IV alone: 680.42 sends the installation back through Parts I and II as well. The Part II items that arrive with it are the ones crews most often miss on a packaged backyard unit:
• Receptacle distances and GFCI protection per 680.22(A) — the receptacle layout and protection are figured the same way as at a pool
• Equipotential bonding per 680.26 for the tub's equipment and the metal within reach of it
• The Part I maintenance disconnecting means: readily accessible, within sight of the equipment it serves, and set back from the inside walls unless separated by a permanent barrier
A listed self-contained unit still lands on a field installation. Its listing covers the tub; the pad wiring, the bonding, the disconnect, and the receptacles around it are installed work under this article.
sections.on_the_job: Price an outdoor spa like a small pool. On a backyard lanai job, the takeoff carries the circuit, the GFCI protection, the bonding, the disconnect, and the receptacle layout as their own line items — the same five lines a pool would get. The tub arriving in one crate changes none of them, and the crew that roughs it in as “just an appliance outlet” is the crew that comes back for the failed inspection.
sections.figure_idea: Lanai spa with callouts: disconnect 5 ft away in sight of the tub, receptacle placed per 680.22(A), bonding conductor tying the tub equipment into the grid.
sections.unverified_reason: Still unverified after Mike Holt recheck (2026-11-25): Two likely errors, not confirmed first-hand. (1) "a factory-built tub does not waive the bonding" overstates it. Since 2017, 680.42 has relieved perimeter-surface equipotential bonding (680.26(B)(2)) for listed self-contained spas/hot tubs installed above a finished surface, under stated conditions, while the tub's own equipment bonding still applies. (2) In NEC 2020 the maintenance disconnecting means appears to be 680.13, not 680.12 (2020 added 680.14 Corrosive Environment and renumbered). Check both against the printed 2020 text, then correct the bullet and the citation.
sections.why_it_exists: A spa puts bathers in a small body of water with pumps, heaters and lights within reach — the same shock hazards as a pool, concentrated. The factory listing can only cover the tub as it left the plant; it cannot cover the pad, the soil, the fence and the receptacles around it. That is why the article pulls the field installation back under the pool rules instead of letting the crate decide.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that a listed, self-contained spa is factory-built, so Part II never shows up and the pad is wired like an appliance outlet. It is wrong: 680.42 sends the installation back through Parts I and II. The listing covers the tub — the installation around it is field work under this article.
inspection_fails: Outdoor spa wired as Part IV only — no equipotential bonding at the tub equipment.
Receptacles placed without checking the 680.22(A) distances and GFCI protection.
Maintenance disconnect not readily accessible, or not within sight of the spa equipment.
Packaged unit set on the pad with no field disconnect — the listing treated as covering the whole installation.

sections.title: Indoor spas and hot tubs
sections.plain_explanation: An indoor spa or hot tub is wired under Parts I and II of Article 680 as modified by 680.43, and any Chapter 3 wiring method may be used. Receptacles [680.43(A)]: at least one 125V, 15A or 20A receptacle on a general-purpose branch circuit must be located not less than 6 ft and not more than 10 ft from the inside wall; every receptacle must be at least 6 ft from the inside walls, measured horizontally; 125-volt receptacles rated 30A or less within 10 ft of the inside walls must be GFCI protected; and a receptacle that supplies spa or hot tub equipment must be GFCI protected. Luminaires and ceiling fans within 5 ft horizontally of an inside wall must be at least 12 ft above the spa or hot tub or be GFCI protected [680.43(B)]. Switches must be at least 5 ft from the inside walls, measured horizontally [680.43(C)] — indoors, no permanent-barrier exception applies to that switch distance; the barrier language in this section belongs to bonding [680.43(D)], which ties together metal parts within 5 ft of the inside walls that are not separated from the spa or hot tub by a permanent barrier. The distances in this section are measured by the shortest path a cord would follow without piercing a floor, wall, ceiling, or other permanent barrier.
sections.on_the_job: Measure the 6 ft receptacle band and the 5 ft switch distance by the cord path around partitions, not a straight line through them — and do not let a partition talk you into a switch inside 5 ft; indoors, the barrier counts for bonding, not for switches.

sections.title: Spas and hot tubs — GFCI protection (680.44)
sections.plain_explanation:
680.44 is the protection rule for spas and hot tubs: the outlet supplying a spa or hot tub must have GFCI protection.
• Read it with the pages around it. The outdoor installations live at 680.42 and the indoor installations at 680.43.
• The protection point, the wiring method and the bonding all have to land together on the same tub — passing the GFCI check alone does not finish the job.
• This page states the NEC 2020 rule Florida enforces. Any 2023 change is confirmed against the printed 2023 text before it is taught here.
sections.on_the_job: On a spa or hot tub hookup, confirm the GFCI protection point before the tub is filled — breaker, receptacle or disconnect device — and test it at final with the tub's own equipment running. Pick the point at rough-in, not at trim: on a backyard spa in Ocala the protection lands at the disconnect the crew installs for the tub, it gets labeled, and the final test runs the pump and heater together so a trip on day one is found by us, not by the homeowner.
sections.unverified_reason: New short page written 2026-11-25 per Mike Holt ruling 8 (the C6 checklists already cite 680.44). Verified=false until checked against the printed NEC 2020.
sections.why_it_exists: A spa concentrates the pool problem into a small tub: a bather sits immersed, surrounded by pumps and a heater, with wet skin that offers very little resistance. A fault in that equipment puts current into water the bather cannot step out of quickly. GFCI protection on the outlet is the personnel protection standing between that fault and the bather.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'the GFCI is in, so the spa passes.' 680.44 is one page of three. The wiring method and the bonding come from 680.42 outdoors or 680.43 indoors, and all of it has to land on the same tub. A protected outlet feeding an indoor tub wired to outdoor rules — or the reverse — is still a failed job.
inspection_fails: Outlet supplying the spa has no GFCI protection — the one thing 680.44 requires.
GFCI device bypassed or replaced with a standard device after nuisance trips.
Tub filled and placed in service before the protection point was confirmed and tested.
Protection point never identified — no breaker, receptacle or disconnect device on the job actually provides the GFCI protection.
Protection tested with the tub empty and off — never proven under the tub's own running equipment.

sections.title: Fountains — Parts I and V
sections.plain_explanation:
Fountains are governed by Part I (general) and Part V of Article 680. The parts are the first decision on the job:
• Decorative fountain nobody enters: Parts I and V.
• Interactive fountain, splash feature, or any fountain people can enter: the Part II rules the section references come in as well — treat the water like a pool.
• The equipment is pool-grade listed equipment: submersible pumps, luminaires, and their supplies. Landscape-lighting stock is not fountain equipment.
• Submersible equipment runs on GFCI protection (680.51(A)) — if it lives under fountain water on line voltage, it is GFCI protected.
sections.on_the_job: An HOA entry fountain in Florida is drawn as a dry-deck ornament, but the site plan shows steps into the basin and the sales brochure calls it a splash feature. That answer changes the wiring: the crew prices it as an enterable fountain, with the referenced Part II rules on top of Parts I and V, a listed submersible pump on GFCI protection, and listed fountain luminaires — not the landscape-lighting package the GC first suggested. Ask about entry before pricing, every time.

nec2023_change.change: Fountains now get the same 5 ft equipment rule as pools: anything above the low-voltage contact limit stays 5 ft from the inside wall unless a permanent barrier separates it. Gear running above the low-voltage contact limit needs at least 5 ft of separation from the fountain's inside wall (680.50(B)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 680.50 Fountain equipment setback

sections.why_it_exists: Water, electricity and bare feet are the pool problem in a smaller basin. A fountain looks harmless because it is shallow and decorative, but a fault in a submersible pump or luminaire puts voltage in water people touch — and on an interactive feature, children stand in it. Pool-grade listed equipment and GFCI protection are what keep a fault from becoming a shock.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that fountains live in Part II with the pools, or that a fountain is just landscape lighting that gets wet. 680.50 puts fountains in Parts I and V; Part II enters only through the reference, when people can get in the water. And the equipment is listed pool-grade equipment — a landscape transformer and a garden luminaire are not a fountain system.
inspection_fails: Landscape-lighting equipment installed as fountain luminaires — not listed fountain equipment.
Submersible pump with no GFCI protection (680.51(A)).
Interactive fountain wired as a dry-deck ornament — the referenced Part II rules were never applied.
Line-voltage equipment in the water that is not listed for fountain use.

sections.title: Fountains — GFCI for submersible equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
Under 680.51(A), GFCI protection is required for fountain luminaires, submersible pumps, and other submersible equipment.
• The one path out: equipment that is part of a listed low-voltage system supplied through the 680.23(A)(2) path.
• If it lives under fountain water and runs on line voltage, it is GFCI protected — no exceptions by habit.
• Fountains are Part V work. A decorative fountain nobody enters runs under Parts I and V; an interactive fountain people can enter pulls in the pool-type rules the article points to as well (680.50).
sections.on_the_job: At rough-in, land every line-voltage fountain pump and luminaire on its GFCI device, and test the protection at startup with water in the basin. A fountain circuit that trips only when wet is a find-it-now problem — do not leave it as a callback or, worse, defeat the device to keep the water feature running. On a Florida decorative fountain at a community entrance, that test happens with the basin full and the pumps running, because a dry test misses the fault that only shows up submerged.
sections.why_it_exists: Fountain equipment lives submerged, in a basin people lean over, reach into, and — on interactive features — wade in. A fault in a submersible pump or luminaire puts voltage into the water itself, and the water spreads it to everyone touching it. GFCI protection is the device that sees that leakage and shuts the circuit off before the basin becomes the hazard.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating fountain gear like landscape lighting — line-voltage submersible equipment on an ordinary circuit because 'it is only a fountain.' 680.51(A) requires GFCI protection for the luminaires, submersible pumps, and other submersible equipment. The trap in the other direction: the listed low-voltage path through 680.23(A)(2) is a real exception, but only for equipment that is actually part of that listed low-voltage system — not for line-voltage gear with a transformer somewhere upstream.
inspection_fails: Submersible fountain pump on a standard breaker — no GFCI protection (680.51(A)).
GFCI device defeated or jumpered out after trips, instead of finding the wet fault.
Landscape-lighting luminaires installed as fountain luminaires — not fountain-grade listed equipment (680.50).
Line-voltage equipment claimed under the low-voltage exception without the listed 680.23(A)(2) system.

page_quiz.explain_plain: 680.51(A) covers the luminaires, the submersible pumps, and the other submersible equipment — unless the listed low-voltage path applies.

page_quiz.question: The exception to 680.51(A) GFCI protection is equipment that is:

page_quiz.explain_plain: The path out is the listed low-voltage system supplied through 680.23(A)(2) — not a habit, and not line-voltage gear with a transformer upstream.

sections.title: Hydromassage bathtubs — Part VII only
sections.plain_explanation:
A hydromassage bathtub — the jetted tub in a bathroom — is governed by Part VII of Article 680 alone. It does not pick up the pool and spa parts.
• The unit goes on an individual branch circuit, with GFCI protection that is readily accessible.
• Receptacles rated 125 V, 30 A or less within 6 ft of the tub need GFCI protection.
• The other electrical equipment in the room stays under Chapters 1 through 4 — that is 680.72.
• The equipment must remain accessible without damaging the building finish (680.73). The access panel is a code item, not a courtesy.
sections.on_the_job: Master-bath remodel in Clermont: the jetted tub's pump lands on its own branch circuit, and because the only receptacle location near the tub is behind the skirt — not readily accessible — the GFCI protection goes in the panel as a GFCI breaker, where anyone can reach and test it. The bidet-seat receptacle 4 ft from the tub rim gets GFCI protection too, under the 6 ft rule. Before tile, the access panel is framed to open fully: pump, junction and disconnect all reachable without cutting the finish, per 680.73.
sections.figure_idea: Jetted tub with access panel open, pump and GFCI visible.
sections.why_it_exists: The bather sits immersed in water that a pump under the tub is pushing through jets. If that pump or its wiring faults, the water and the wet bather are the path. GFCI protection on a dedicated circuit is the personnel protection, and the access rule exists because a pump nobody can reach is a pump nobody inspects, services or disconnects when it starts to fail.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer treats the jetted tub like a small spa and reaches for the pool and spa parts — bonding grids, Part II distances, the works. A hydromassage bathtub lives in Part VII alone: individual branch circuit, readily accessible GFCI, GFCI on receptacles within 6 ft, and real access to the equipment. The other trap is hiding the GFCI behind the tub, where it can never be reached or tested.
inspection_fails: Tub pump on a shared bathroom circuit — 680.71 requires an individual branch circuit.
GFCI receptacle installed behind the tub skirt where it cannot be reached or tested — protection must be readily accessible.

Standard receptacle 4 ft from the tub with no GFCI protection.

sections.title: Pool lifts — Part VIII
sections.plain_explanation:
Part VIII of Article 680 covers electrically operated pool lifts — the accessibility lifts at commercial and amenity pools (the lift is defined in 680.2). Only Part I and Part VIII apply to the lift itself; the rest of Article 680 does not ride along.
• The lift must be listed, labeled and identified for swimming pool and spa use.
• A lift connected to premises wiring and operating above the low-voltage contact limit gets GFCI protection for personnel.
• The lift is bonded into the pool's equipotential bonding system — metal fittings attached to the pool structure under 680.26(B)(5) and fixed metal parts under 680.26(B)(7), with solid copper not smaller than 8 AWG.
• The listing exceptions are narrow: lifts running on a removable battery that is charged away from the pool, and small solar lifts, sit outside the listing rule. Read the exception before assuming one covers your lift.
sections.on_the_job: Amenity-pool ADA work at a Florida apartment community: the lift is electrical scope — include its circuit and bonding in the pool price, not as an afterthought allowance. On the rough-in that means a GFCI-protected circuit to the lift location and an 8 AWG solid copper bonding jumper tying the lift into the equipotential grid with the ladders and handrails. If the specified lift is a removable-battery model charged in the pump room, confirm the exception actually fits before deleting the circuit from the bid.

sections.why_it_exists: The lift carries a person with limited mobility into the water on a metal machine connected to premises power. If a fault energizes the frame, that user cannot jump clear. Listing proves the machine was built for wet service, GFCI protection cuts a ground fault in milliseconds, and bonding holds the lift, the water and the deck at one potential so no voltage difference can drive current through the swimmer.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating the lift like pool furniture the GC sets in place — 'not electrical.' Part VIII makes it listed electrical equipment with GFCI and bonding duties. The reverse trap is bonding the lift back to the panelboard: equipotential bonding ties the lift to the pool's bonding system, and bonding jumpers in the pool area are not required to run back to a remote panel, service or electrode.
inspection_fails: Lift set and powered with no bonding jumper to the pool's equipotential grid.
Lift circuit on a plain breaker — no GFCI protection for personnel.
Unlisted residential-grade lift installed at a commercial amenity pool.
Bonding jumper landed only on the branch-circuit equipment ground and never tied into the pool bonding system.

sections.title: Article 682 — Natural and Artificially Made Bodies of Water
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 682 covers electrical installations in and around natural and artificially made bodies of water that are not pools or fountains — lakes, ponds, and similar bodies of water.
• In scope: floating structures, equipment near the water's edge, and docks that fall outside Article 555's scope.
• Out of scope: pools, spas, and fountains — those stay in Article 680.
• The 2020 shoreline location rule puts service equipment 5 ft back from the water, with live parts 12 in above the datum plane — the reference level the article measures heights from.
• The shock-hazard logic follows Article 680's thinking: GFCI protection, grounding and bonding discipline, and heights above the water figured before anything is set.
Florida lakefront work lands here.
sections.on_the_job: On lakefront work, treat every receptacle and piece of equipment near the waterline as shock-hazard work: GFCI protection, bonding of the metal parts, and heights above the water figured before anything is set. On a Florida lake house, that means the shoreline equipment is laid out 5 ft back with live parts 12 in above the datum plane before the trench is dug — not adjusted after the pad is poured. Where a dock is involved, Article 555 may govern instead of or alongside this article — ask Mike which one controls before rough-in.

nec2023_change.change: Distribution equipment on land, feeder equipment included, now falls under the shoreline location rule that once covered only service equipment: 5 ft back, live parts 12 in above the datum plane. The location rules now cover distribution equipment on land, feeder equipment included, not just the service equipment.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 682.11 Equipment location near shorelines

nec2023_change.change: Floating structures can now have splices between the waterline and the datum plane if they're submersion-rated, and replacement connections in that zone must be listed and identified for submersion. Floating structures: splices can now sit below the datum plane, as long as they stay above the waterline.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 682.12 Splices and connections near water

nec2023_change.change: Near natural and man-made bodies of water, every metal enclosure, equipment frame and receptacle grounding terminal ties to an equipment grounding conductor run with the circuit conductors. Metal boxes, cabinets and enclosures, metal frames of utilization equipment, and receptacle grounding terminals all connect to the equipment grounding conductor (EGC).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 682.31 Equipment grounding near bodies of water

sections.why_it_exists: Open water has no walls, no floor, and no safe edge — a person in a lake touches the water, the dock, and the boat at the same time, and a fault anywhere in that system has all of them to travel through. The article exists because the pool rules stop at the pool wall, but the shock hazard does not.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is reaching for Article 680 because there is water. A lake is not a pool: 682 covers natural and artificially made bodies of water, and its shoreline rules are measured from the datum plane, not from the deck or the seawall cap. The second trap is assuming a dock is always 682 work — a marina or boatyard dock can be Article 555 work instead, and the two articles do not ask for the same installation.

sections.title: Article 685 — Integrated Electrical Systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 685 covers integrated electrical systems — unitized segments of an industrial wiring system where an orderly shutdown is necessary to ensure safe operation. It is not a size or voltage class. A system only qualifies when all three conditions in 685.1 are met at the same time:
• An orderly shutdown is required to minimize personnel hazard and equipment damage — killing power suddenly is itself the danger.
• Conditions of maintenance and supervision ensure that qualified persons service the system, and the names of those qualified persons are kept in a permanent record at the office in charge of the installation.
• Effective safeguards acceptable to the authority having jurisdiction are established and maintained.
Where a system qualifies, the article relaxes a few normal rules so a fault alarm can be answered with a planned shutdown instead of a trip:
• 685.10: overcurrent devices critical to the system may be accessible rather than readily accessible, mounted at heights that keep unqualified personnel from operating them.
• 685.12: two-wire dc circuits are permitted to be ungrounded.
• 685.14: control circuits of 150 volts or less from separately derived systems are permitted to be ungrounded where operational continuity is required.
Table 685.3 in 685.3 points to the sections in other articles — 430.44 for motors is one — that carry their own orderly-shutdown provisions.
sections.on_the_job: Recognition only. Sharma's work is houses and small commercial, so this article shows up for us as a reading skill, not an installation method: where a facility's drawings show an integrated electrical system, its orderly-shutdown documentation is part of the electrical record — keep it with the panel directories in the job file, and do not rewire interconnections between systems without the engineer of record. If a service call ever takes a crew into a plant that runs under 685, the first question is who the named qualified persons are; if nobody can produce that record, the system is not being run the way the article requires.
sections.why_it_exists: In a chemical plant, a steel mill, or over a scrap yard, sudden power loss is not the safe state — it is the accident. A lifting electromagnet drops its load, a reaction runs away, molten metal freezes in the wrong place. Article 685 trades the normal accessibility and grounding rules for supervision: alarms announce a fault, and trained people shut the process down in sequence before anyone gets hurt.
sections.exam_trap: The exam trap is "any large industrial service." Article 685 is not about size — a big plant that fails any one of the three 685.1 conditions is wired under the normal rules, readily accessible overcurrent devices and grounded systems included.
inspection_fails: Qualified persons' names missing from the permanent record at the office in charge of the installation (685.1).
Safeguards for the integrated system not established, not maintained, or never accepted by the AHJ (685.1).
Critical overcurrent devices moved down to readily accessible height during a later alteration, defeating the security 685.10 allows.
Interconnections between systems rewired in the field with no engineer of record and no update to the shutdown documentation.

sections.title: Article 690 — Solar Photovoltaic (PV) Systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 690 covers PV systems from the module terminals to the point of connection with the premises wiring:
• Circuit current is figured under 690.8, and conductors and overcurrent devices are sized under 690.8 and 690.9.
• Maximum voltage is set by 690.7, calculated from module open-circuit voltage corrected for the coldest expected temperature; on one- and two-family dwellings the maximum system voltage is 600 V.
• Ground-fault protection is at 690.41(B) and arc-fault protection at 690.11. The old 690.5 ground-fault number was deleted in the 2020 edition.
• Rapid shutdown on buildings is 690.12. The array boundary is 1 ft from the array in all directions. Outside the boundary, controlled conductors are limited to not more than 30 V within 30 seconds of initiation; inside it, not more than 80 V within 30 seconds, or a listed PV hazard control system.
• Disconnecting means are at 690.13 and 690.15.
• Marking is 690.56: plaques and directories that tell the next electrician — and the fire department — what the system is and where it shuts off. The rapid-shutdown label sits on or within 3 ft of the service disconnecting means.
• Interconnection to the premises system runs through Article 705: the 120% bus rule lives at 705.12(B)(3)(2) in Chapter 7 and is deliberately not repeated here.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma's solar-adjacent work is mostly service, additions, and builder rough-ins that a solar contractor finishes. On a new Marion County home, Sharma's part is the service: Siemens meter-main, the rapid-shutdown initiation point at the service equipment, and the 690.56 label on or within 3 ft of the disconnect — so the solar contractor's array lands on a service that already shuts down and reads correctly. The disconnect, marking, and rapid-shutdown pages are the ones that decide whose inspection fails.

The NEC 2023 changes in this article apply in Florida to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026 (FBC 9th Ed.); earlier permits stay on NEC 2020.

Floating PV, whether the gear rides on the water itself or mounts to something that floats, must be identified for that use (690.4(G)).

sections.why_it_exists: A PV array makes its own power whenever the sun is up — there is no switch on a module. The article exists so a second power source on the building can be shut down, marked, and kept from backfeeding people who believe the building is dead: firefighters working the roof, and the next electrician at the panel. The voltage limits inside the array boundary protect the person cutting a vent hole over live conductors.
sections.exam_trap: Two traps live on this page. First: "the 120% bus rule is part of Article 690." It is not — interconnection runs through Article 705, and the rule sits at 705.12(B)(3)(2). Second: quoting the old 690.5 for PV ground-fault protection. That number was deleted in the 2020 edition; ground-fault protection is now at 690.41(B).
inspection_fails: Rapid-shutdown label missing, or more than 3 ft from the service disconnecting means.
Conductors inside the array boundary still above 80 V thirty seconds after initiation.

sections.title: Ground-fault protection (690.41(B) in 2020; the old 690.5 was deleted)
sections.plain_explanation:
PV systems must be provided with ground-fault protection that meets 690.41(B). The protection has three jobs:
• Detect a ground fault in the DC circuits.
• Interrupt the faulted circuit.
• Indicate that the fault happened.
The equipment must be listed for PV ground-fault protection. In 2020 this protection lives at 690.41(B) — the old 690.5 address was deleted, so a spec or plan note that still cites 690.5 is citing a dead number. This is the DC-side companion to 690.11's arc-fault protection: a ground fault is current leaking out of the circuit to ground, while a series arc is a break arcing inside the circuit. They are different failures, and one device does not cover both.
sections.why_it_exists: A PV array is current-limited: a ground fault on a roof may never draw enough current to open an overcurrent device, so it can sit there heating for weeks. Wet mornings make it worse — dew gives the fault a path it does not have at noon. Detection, interruption, and a visible indication are what turn a silent roof-fire risk into a service call.
sections.on_the_job: Service call on a rooftop system in Winter Garden: the inverter shows a ground-fault indication and has shut down. That indication is 690.41(B) doing its third job, so the crew treats it as a find-the-fault call, not a reset-and-leave call. They work the DC circuits string by string until the faulted string shows itself — chafed insulation where a conductor leaves the array is the usual Florida find, with sun and roof heat doing the damage. The fault gets repaired and the insulation verified; only then does the system go back in service. Resetting without finding it just schedules the fire for later.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer cites 690.5 — deleted in 2020; ground-fault protection moved to 690.41(B). Second trap: swapping in arc-fault protection. 690.11 answers series arcs in DC circuits operating at 80 V dc or more; it does not detect a ground fault, and ground-fault protection does not interrupt a series arc. Each section is owed on its own.

sections.title: Maximum voltage — correct Voc for cold
sections.plain_explanation:
A PV string's voltage is not its nameplate total. Module open-circuit voltage rises as temperature falls, so maximum system voltage is calculated from the sum of the series modules' rated open-circuit voltages corrected to the lowest expected ambient temperature at the site, using a method 690.7(A) allows: the manufacturer's temperature coefficient of Voc from the module listing instructions, or the correction factors of Table 690.7(A) for crystalline and multicrystalline silicon modules. The corrected voltage must not exceed the rated voltage of the connected equipment (inverter input, disconnects, conductors), and maximum PV system voltage for one- and two-family dwellings is limited to 600V.

Table 690.7(A) correction factors (crystalline and multicrystalline silicon modules), by lowest expected ambient temperature:
• 4°C to 0°C — 1.10
• −1°C to −5°C — 1.12
• −6°C to −10°C — 1.14
• −11°C to −15°C — 1.16
• −16°C to −20°C — 1.18
• −21°C to −25°C — 1.20
Florida's lowest expected ambient temperatures usually fall in the 1.02–1.12 rows; use the site's design low (e.g., the ASHRAE extreme annual mean minimum, per the Informational Note) — but the factor is taken from the site's lowest expected temperature, not from the weather on install day. Warmer Table 690.7(A) rows used in central and south Florida: 24 to 20°C — 1.02; 19 to 15°C — 1.04; 14 to 10°C — 1.06; 9 to 5°C — 1.08 (above the 4 to 0°C row at 1.10). 690.7(A)(3): systems with inverter generating capacity of 100 kW or more may use a documented, stamped engineering method — PE design required; flag for Sanjay.
sections.on_the_job: Size the string on the coldest bright morning of the year, not on the day of the install — over-voltage on a frosty sunrise is the failure this section exists to prevent.
sections.figure_idea: Thermometer at dawn beside an array; Voc arrow rising as the temperature falls; 600V dwelling cap marked.

sections.title: Circuit current and conductor sizing
sections.plain_explanation:
PV current is figured on the article's own multipliers, not on load estimates.
• 690.8(A): the maximum current for a PV source circuit is the sum of the parallel module short-circuit currents multiplied by 125%.
• 690.8(B): conductors are then sized at the larger of two numbers — 125% of the (A) current before any temperature correction or adjustment factors, or 100% of the (A) current after those factors are applied.
Both checks must be run. Either one can govern, depending on the rooftop temperature and the conduit fill.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example, Florida rooftop. Two parallel strings of modules with an Isc of 10.4 A each: the maximum current under 690.8(A) is (10.4 + 10.4) × 1.25 = 26 A. Check 1: 26 × 1.25 = 32.5 A before factors — 10 AWG copper at 75 °C (35 A, Table 310.16) passes. Check 2: on this roof the temperature correction and adjustment factors multiply out to 0.70, so the conductor needs 26 ÷ 0.70 = 37.1 A of table ampacity to still deliver 26 A after derating — 10 AWG falls short, and 8 AWG (50 A) governs. Do the two-step check on paper; hot Florida rooftops make the after-correction figure govern more often than installers expect.
sections.figure_idea: Worksheet sketch: parallel Isc sum × 1.25, then the two conductor checks side by side.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A PV array in full sun delivers its current for hours without cycling — it behaves as a continuous load on a hot roof, the worst combination a conductor ever sees. The first multiplier covers the array making more current than its summed nameplates suggest; the two-check sizing then covers the conductor carrying less than its table value once rooftop heat and conduit fill are counted. Skip either side and the wire becomes the fuse.
inspection_fails: PV source-circuit conductors sized from module operating current (Imp) instead of the parallel Isc sum multiplied by 125%.
Worksheet shows the Isc sum carried straight to Table 310.16 — the 690.8(A) maximum current was never figured.
Only the before-factors check run: rooftop temperature correction and adjustment factors never applied, so the conductors fail the 690.8(B) after-factors check.
Ampacity read from the 90 °C column for equipment whose terminations are rated 75 °C (110.14(C)).
sections.exam_trap: The trap is stopping after the first check — '32.5 A, and 10 AWG is 35 A, done.' On a hot roof, the after-factors check can demand more than the before-factors number, and it governs. The mirror-image error is sizing from the modules' operating current (Imp) instead of the parallel short-circuit sum: 690.8 starts from Isc, every time.

page_quiz.question: Two parallel strings, Isc 10.4 A each: the 690.8(A) maximum current is:
page_quiz.explain_plain: (10.4 + 10.4) × 1.25 = 26 A. The 32.5 A figure is check 1 of the conductor sizing, not the (A) current.

page_quiz.question: Under 690.8(B), conductors are sized at:
choices: 125% of the Isc sum, with no second check
The larger of 125% of (A) before factors, or 100% of (A) after factors
page_quiz.explain_plain: Both checks run; the larger result buys the wire. Rooftop heat decides which one governs.

page_quiz.question: Check 1 needs 32.5 A and check 2 needs 37.1 A of table ampacity. The minimum copper conductor at 75 °C is:
page_quiz.explain_plain: The governing number is 37.1 A. Table 310.16 at 75 °C: 10 AWG is 35 A — short — so 8 AWG at 50 A is the pick.

sections.title: Overcurrent protection
sections.plain_explanation:
Where overcurrent protection is required for a PV circuit, the device rating is not less than 125% of the maximum current figured under 690.8(A) — the sum of the parallel module short-circuit currents multiplied by 125%.
• No overcurrent device is required at all where two conditions both hold: the conductors are sized for the full available current, and no external source can backfeed current beyond their ampacity.
• Parallel strings are the usual external source. One string cannot overdrive its own conductors; two or more strings can drive current backward into a faulted third string.
• String fusing questions are answered by applying those two conditions, not by habit — 'we always fuse' and 'we never fuse' are both wrong answers.
sections.on_the_job: Three or more parallel strings is where the backfeed condition usually starts to bite — check it before deciding fuses are 'never needed' or 'always needed.' On a Florida rooftop with three strings of modules at 9.8 amperes short-circuit current each: one string's maximum current is 9.8 × 125% = 12.25 amperes. If that string faults, the other two strings can backfeed about 24.5 amperes into it — beyond what conductors sized for one string can carry — so the strings get fuses, each rated not less than 125% of the 690.8(A) current.

nec2023_change.change: Revised language in Section 690.9(D), providing a pointer to 705.30(F), where specific requirements applicable to interconnected systems are addressed.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 690.9(0) Transformers

sections.why_it_exists: A PV module is current-limited — a shorted string does not make big fault current by itself. The danger is the rest of the array: parallel strings, and any interconnected source, will drive current backward into a faulted string's conductors, past what those conductors can carry, for as long as the sun shines. The fuse is there to open that backfeed path before the conductor becomes the fuse.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is answering string-fuse questions from habit. 'PV never needs fuses because modules are current-limited' forgets the backfeed from the parallel strings. 'Every string always gets a fuse' ignores the two-condition case where no device is required at all. The exam wants the conditions applied: conductors sized for the full available current, and no external source able to backfeed beyond their ampacity.

tables.caption: 690.9 — the two-condition test for no overcurrent device
rows: Conductors sized for full available current
Ampacity covers every current the circuit can see
No parallel strings or other source can push current back in
Provide the device — rated ≥ 125% of the 690.8(A) current

inspection_fails: Three parallel strings combined with no string fuses and conductors sized for one string — backfeed path unprotected (690.9).
Overcurrent device rated below 125% of the maximum current figured under 690.8(A).
Fuses omitted because 'modules are current-limited,' where parallel strings can backfeed the faulted string.
A fuse installed by habit on a circuit that meets both no-device conditions, then blamed for nuisance openings — the conditions were never checked either way.

page_quiz.question: Where overcurrent protection is required for a PV circuit, the device rating must be not less than:
choices: 125% of the maximum current figured under 690.8(A)
The next size above the conductor size
page_quiz.explain_plain: 690.9 ties the device rating to the 690.8(A) maximum current — not less than 125% of it.

page_quiz.question: No overcurrent device is required for a PV circuit when:
choices: The array has only one string, always
Conductors are sized for the full available current AND no external source can backfeed beyond their ampacity
page_quiz.explain_plain: Both conditions must hold together — conductor ampacity for the full available current, and no external source able to backfeed beyond that ampacity.

page_quiz.question: Why do three parallel strings change the fuse answer?
choices: The healthy strings can backfeed a faulted string beyond its conductor ampacity
Fuses are required by the module warranty
They do not — string count never matters
page_quiz.explain_plain: One string cannot overdrive its own conductors, but the other parallel strings drive current backward into a fault — that backfeed is what the fuse opens.

sections.title: Arc-fault circuit protection (DC)
sections.plain_explanation:
PV systems with DC circuits operating at 80 V dc or greater between any two conductors must be protected by a listed PV arc-fault circuit interrupter, or by other listed system components providing equivalent protection.
• The protection must detect and interrupt arcing faults caused by a failure in the intended continuity of a conductor, connection, module, or other component in the PV DC circuits.
• Exception: systems not installed on or in buildings, where the DC circuits are in metallic raceways or metal-clad cables, in enclosed metallic cable trays, or underground.
sections.on_the_job: Rooftop retrofit in Orlando: the string voltage is far over the 80 V trigger, so the inverter's listed PV AFCI is not an option — it is the protection, and it stays enabled. The crew's part is connector discipline: matched, fully seated connectors, because a loose series connection is the classic arc source. Across town, a ground-mounted array at a warehouse keeps its DC runs underground and in metallic raceway and is not on or in a building — that is the shape of the exception.
sections.figure_idea: Series arc at a failed connection, AFCI device interrupting the string.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A DC arc does not pass through zero 120 times a second the way AC does, so once a failing connector starts arcing it tends to keep arcing — a small, very hot plasma sitting on a roof or in a junction box. The current is normal load current, so no breaker or fuse sees a fault. The AFCI watches the circuit's signature, recognizes the arc, and shuts the string down before the connection point burns through.
inspection_fails: PV system on a home with DC circuits over 80 V and no listed arc-fault protection, or the inverter's AFCI function disabled.
Exception claimed for a rooftop array because conductors are in metallic raceway — the array is on a building.
Mismatched or incompletely seated PV connectors left as a series-arc source.
AC dwelling AFCI breaker offered as the 690.11 protection for a DC string.
sections.exam_trap: Two traps. First, reaching for 210.12: that is AC branch-circuit AFCI for dwelling rooms and has nothing to do with PV DC circuits. Second, claiming the exception for a rooftop array because the conductors are in EMT — the exception starts with 'not installed on or in buildings,' and a rooftop array fails that test before the raceway question is even asked.

page_quiz.explain_plain: The trigger is 80 V dc or greater between any two conductors.

page_quiz.explain_plain: 690.11 targets series arcing from failed continuity in the DC circuits.

sections.title: Rapid shutdown of PV systems on buildings
sections.plain_explanation:
Rapid shutdown controls PV conductors on and in buildings, so firefighters can work around a live array. The sun keeps the modules energized; this section caps what the conductors may carry once shutdown is initiated.
• The array boundary is 1 ft from the array in all directions.
• Outside the boundary — and for conductors more than 3 ft from the point of entry into the building — controlled conductors must be limited to not more than 30 V within 30 seconds of initiation.
• Inside the boundary, use one of the section's paths: a listed PV hazard control system (PVHCS, UL 3741); or conductors limited to not more than 80 V within 30 seconds; or an array with no exposed wiring methods or conductive parts, installed not less than 8 ft from exposed grounded conductive parts.
The initiation device is covered at 690.12(C), and the labels at 690.56.
sections.on_the_job: On a Florida rooftop residential job, Sharma's standard path is module-level shutdown electronics, initiated at the PV disconnect beside the Siemens meter-main on the exterior wall — the 690.12(C) device a firefighter can find without entering the house. The reflective red RAPID SHUTDOWN label goes on or within 3 ft of that device, in capital letters at least 3/8 in. high (690.56). Thirty seconds after initiation, a meter on the conductors leaving the boundary must read 30 V or less. That check is what the inspector and the fire crew are really buying.
sections.figure_idea: Roof plan: array, 1 ft boundary line, conductor leaving the boundary tagged '30V in 30 s.'

nec2023_change.change: Carports, parking shades and other open detached structures can now carry PV without rapid shutdown. The third inside-array option is gone, and the building label moved into 690.12(D). New Exception No. 2: PV on nonenclosed detached structures, such as carports, parking shade structures and solar trellises, skips rapid shutdown.

sections.why_it_exists: A fire crew venting a roof or cutting an opening works blind, in smoke, around conductors that stay live as long as light hits the modules — there is no switch at the sun. Without rapid shutdown, a saw through a PV conductor can put full array voltage on the crew. Dropping the conductors outside the array to 30 V within 30 seconds, and capping or listing the hazard inside the boundary, makes the roof a place firefighters can work.
inspection_fails: No rapid shutdown label at the service disconnect or initiation device, or the label sits more than 3 ft away from it (690.56).
Label letters under 3/8 in. high, or not white capitals on a red reflective background (690.56(C)(2)).
Initiation device for a one- or two-family dwelling located inside the building instead of at a readily accessible outdoor location (690.12(C)).
Conductors outside the array boundary still over 30 V thirty seconds after initiation — module electronics not paired or not commissioned.
The 2023 carport exception applied on a job permitted under NEC 2020, leaving detached-structure PV with no rapid shutdown.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is applying the 30 V limit everywhere. Inside the array boundary, the 2020 limit is 80 V within 30 seconds — or a listed PVHCS, or the no-exposed-parts path. The other wrong answer is placing the boundary at the edge of the modules: it sits 1 ft out, in all directions.

sections.title: Rapid shutdown initiation device
sections.plain_explanation:
The initiation device is the switch that starts rapid shutdown (690.12). It has to pass three checks:
• Readily accessible — reachable fast, without a ladder, a locked gate, or a trip through the building.
• It clearly indicates whether it is in the off position (shutdown initiated) or the on position.
• It may be the service disconnect, the PV system disconnect, or another listed switch — no special device is required.
For one- and two-family dwellings, the initiation device must be located at a readily accessible location outside the building — the fire crew does not enter the house to shut the array down. What initiation buys, per 690.12: outside the array boundary, controlled conductors are limited to not more than 30 V within 30 seconds; inside the boundary, not more than 80 V within 30 seconds, unless a listed PV hazard control system is used.
sections.on_the_job: On dwelling jobs, walk out front and find the initiation point the way a firefighter would — if you can't, neither can they. Sharma's standard layout puts the PV disconnect beside the Siemens meter-main on the exterior wall and makes that disconnect the initiation device: one throw, ON and OFF positions marked, and the reflective red RAPID SHUTDOWN label on or within 3 ft of it, with letters at least 3/8 in. high (690.56(C)). After initiation, the conductors leaving the array boundary must be down to 30 V or less within 30 seconds — that is the number the fire crew is counting on.
sections.figure_idea: Initiation switch beside the meter on an exterior wall, placard visible from the driveway.
sections.why_it_exists: Sunlight keeps a PV array energized even with the utility service off, and firefighters work on and around those roofs. Rapid shutdown only protects them if the first firefighter on scene can find and throw the initiation device in seconds, from outside, and tell at a glance whether shutdown is on. A device hidden in a garage or an unlabeled switch fails the whole purpose of 690.12.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is naming the inverter's built-in switch, or a disconnect inside the garage, as the initiation device on a dwelling. Both fail the rule: for one- and two-family dwellings the device must be at a readily accessible location outside the building, and it must show its position clearly.
inspection_fails: Initiation device inside the garage or the house on a one- or two-family dwelling.
Switch with no clear ON/OFF indication of the shutdown state.
No reflective rapid-shutdown label at the device, or label letters under 3/8 in. high.
Device behind a locked gate, a fence, or landscaping — not readily accessible.

tables.caption: What initiation must deliver (690.12)
tables.note: Inside the boundary, a listed PV hazard control system (PVHCS) is the other path. The array boundary is 1 ft from the array in all directions.

sections.title: PV system disconnecting means
sections.plain_explanation:
Means shall be provided to disconnect the PV system from all wiring systems — the utility power system, any energy storage system, and the utilization equipment and its premises wiring. The disconnecting means has to pass three checks:
• Be installed at a readily accessible location (690.13(A)) — reachable quickly, without a ladder, a locked room, or a trip through the building.
• Plainly indicate whether it is in the open (off) or closed (on) position (690.13(B)).
• Be permanently marked "PV SYSTEM DISCONNECT" (690.13(B)) — a real marking that survives the weather, not tape or marker.
Where all the terminals of the disconnect can still be energized with the switch open — the array side stays live in sunlight — a warning sign goes on or next to the disconnect. Where the PV disconnect is not at the service equipment, the directory and plaque rules of 690.56 point back to where it is, so every source at the building can be found from the service.
sections.on_the_job: Rooftop PV on a Florida house: the inverter sits on the garage wall and the crew lands the PV system disconnect outside, beside the Siemens meter-main, where it is readily accessible from grade. It is a real switch that shows OPEN and ON, permanently marked PV SYSTEM DISCONNECT. Because it is grouped at the service, the 690.56 plaque at the same spot names it with the building's other sources. The homeowner is told plainly: the switch kills the connection, but the panels and their leads stay live in daylight.
sections.why_it_exists: A PV array makes power whenever light hits it, so opening the utility breaker does not make the solar side safe. The disconnect is the one place a firefighter, a utility crew, or the next electrician can separate the PV system from every other wiring system and know it is open. If it is hidden, unmarked, or ambiguous about its position, somebody works on conductors they believe are dead that are not.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is answering that the rapid shutdown switch, or the inverter's own control, satisfies 690.13. Rapid shutdown (690.12) limits conductor voltage for firefighters; it is not the PV system disconnecting means. 690.13 wants a disconnecting means that separates the PV system from all wiring systems, sits where it is readily accessible, plainly shows open or closed, and is permanently marked PV SYSTEM DISCONNECT.
inspection_fails: PV disconnect inside the attic or behind a locked gate — not readily accessible (690.13(A)).
Disconnect marked with tape or a marker — the marking is not permanent (690.13(B)).
Switch gives no plain indication of open versus closed position (690.13(B)).
PV disconnect remote from the service, with no directory or plaque at the service equipment pointing to it (690.56).

sections.title: Disconnection of PV equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
690.15 is about isolating one piece of PV equipment — an inverter, a charge controller, a dc-to-dc converter — so it can be serviced or replaced with every source cut off. The disconnecting means must open all ungrounded conductors from all sources:
• The array side. The modules make power whenever there is light; opening the ac side does nothing to the dc input.
• The utility side. The grid backfeeds the inverter's ac terminals until its ac disconnect is opened.
• The storage side, on hybrid systems with batteries.
Location (2020): the isolating device or equipment disconnect goes in the equipment, or within sight and within 10 ft of it. Where it sits farther away, it must be capable of being locked in the open position (110.25). An isolating device that is not rated to interrupt the circuit current must be marked "Do Not Disconnect Under Load."
sections.on_the_job: Before opening an inverter, verify both sides are dead — the array makes power whenever the sun is up. On a Florida rooftop hybrid job that is three checks, not two: open the dc disconnect at the inverter and meter the array input, open the ac disconnect and meter the output, and open the battery disconnect on the storage side. The 690.15 disconnects sit at the inverter — within sight and within 10 ft — so the tech who opened them can see them from the equipment while the cover is off.

nec2023_change.change: Rearranged 690.15 with some grammatical changes. A requirement for an equipment disconnecting means to be within 10 feet of the equipment to now be within sight was also modified.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 690.15 Disconnecting Means for Isolating Photovoltaic Equipment

sections.why_it_exists: PV equipment is fed from directions that do not behave like a normal circuit. There is no switch on the sun: an inverter whose ac side is off still has live dc at its terminals in full daylight, and a hybrid inverter adds a battery that never sleeps. This section exists so the person opening the equipment can put every one of those sources behind an open, visible disconnect first.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is 'the PV system disconnect is off, so the inverter is safe to open.' The 690.13 system disconnect separates the system from the building and the grid; it does nothing about the array wired straight into the inverter's dc terminals. Rapid shutdown (690.12) is the other wrong answer — it limits conductor voltage for firefighters, it does not isolate equipment for service. 690.15 isolation is per piece of equipment, from every source.

tables.caption: Two different disconnect jobs
rows: At the equipment, or within sight + 10 ft

sections.title: Wiring methods — PV source and output circuits
sections.plain_explanation:
690.31 is where solar wiring stops being ordinary branch-circuit wiring. Exposed single-conductor PV source-circuit wiring is a listed PV cable type (Type PV wire, or USE-2 where the section permits it) — conductors built and marked for sunlight, heat, and rooftop duty, not THHN pulled out of a raceway and left in the sun. Rooftop conductors also live in the hottest part of the job, which is why the temperature rules of Chapter 3 ride along. Where inside a building, PV system DC circuits over 30V or 8A must be in metal raceways, in Type MC cable that complies with 250.118(10), or in metal enclosures, from the point of penetration into the building to the first readily accessible disconnecting means (690.31(D)) — so a dc fault inside a wall is contained in metal. The rule applies inside buildings, not to runs on the building. Module interconnects, home runs, and the inverter output each follow the part of the section written for them — read the subsection for the run in front of you.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 690.31(B): Section 690.31(B) was revised and a new list item (1), Conductors of Different Systems, was added while the previous text in that location was moved to list item (2), Identification. The text revisions provide conditions where PV dc circuits and inverter output circuits can now be installed in the same junction box, pull box or wireway provided they are identified, grouped, and separated in accordance with 690.31 (B)(2) and (B)(3).
• 690.31(B)(1): Exception revised to permit the dc and ac conductors of a PV system to be located within the same enclosure where all the conductors are insulated for the highest voltage present and grouped appropriately.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: On a roof: PV wire for the exposed home runs, secured and kept off the roof surface the way the listing expects, then into metal raceway where the dc run enters and crosses the building to the inverter. Loose THHN or cable not listed for the exposure, lying on a Florida roof, is a failed inspection and a cooked conductor.

sections.title: Grounding electrode system — PV ties into the building system
sections.plain_explanation: A PV installation does not get its own separate grounding world. 690.47 ties the array's equipment grounding and any dc grounding electrode conductor into the building's grounding electrode system, so the array, the service, and everything else bonded in the building sit at the same potential. An additional electrode at the array — a ground rod driven by the racking — is permitted, but it supplements the system: it is an auxiliary electrode under 690.47(B) and 250.54. It may connect directly to the array frame or structure, and it does not have to be bonded to the building GES, because the bonding path back to the service is the array's equipment grounding conductor (Part VII of Article 250). The earth is never the fault-current path., and it never replaces that connection. A rod in the dirt by the array with no bond back to the service is a decoration, not a grounding electrode system. A rod with no EGC path back to the service is not compliant: the array equipment grounding conductors connect to the building's grounding electrode system per 690.47(A).
sections.on_the_job: Ground-mount or roof array: bond the racking and equipment back to the house grounding electrode system, and if the design adds a rod at the array, bond that rod in too. The inspector's question is always the same — show me the path back to the service ground.
sections.figure_idea: Array grounding: racking bond, conductor back to the service grounding electrode system, optional auxiliary rod bonded in.

sections.title: Marking — plaques, directories, and the rapid shutdown label
sections.plain_explanation:
PV systems carry permanent plaques and directories so every source at a building can be found from the service equipment:
• A stand-alone system follows the directory rule of 710.10
• A system interconnected with another source follows 705.10
• A permanent label on or within 3 ft of the service disconnecting means states that the system is equipped with rapid shutdown and carries the 690.56(C) diagram showing the switch locations
• A reflective label on or within 3 ft of the rapid shutdown initiation device reads RAPID SHUTDOWN SWITCH FOR SOLAR PV SYSTEM — capital letters at least 3/8 in. high, white on red (690.56(C)(2))
Marking is not paperwork; it is the part of the system the fire department uses.
sections.on_the_job: Orlando rooftop retrofit: the Siemens service panel gets the directory plaque naming the PV source, the rapid-shutdown label with the roof diagram goes on the meter-main — within 3 ft of the service disconnect — and the reflective RAPID SHUTDOWN SWITCH label goes at the initiation device by the front door. Carry the red RSD labels in the truck stock — a missing 3/8 in. label fails finals, and the re-inspection trip costs more than the roll of labels.
sections.figure_idea: Red-and-white rapid shutdown placard beside the service disconnect, letters dimensioned 3/8 in.

nec2023_change.change: The building rapid shutdown label moved out of 690.56(C) into 690.12(D). What stays in 690.56 is power source identification by plaque or directory. The building rapid shutdown label, with its simple roof diagram, moved from 690.56(C) to 690.12(D).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 690.56 Rapid shutdown label moved

sections.why_it_exists: A PV array is a power source that stays live in daylight even with the service open. Firefighters on a roof and linemen at the service have to find every source and shut the array down fast: the directory tells them the sources exist, and the red rapid-shutdown label tells them where the switch is. A missing label means crews treat the whole roof as energized.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is letter size and placement from memory: 1/4 in. letters, or the label stuck anywhere on the building. The initiation-device label needs capitals at least 3/8 in. high, white on red, reflective, on or within 3 ft of the device — and the service label lives on or within 3 ft of the service disconnecting means.

sections.title: Article 691 — Large-Scale Photovoltaic (PV) Electric Supply Stations
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 691 covers large-scale photovoltaic (PV) electric supply stations — utility-scale PV plants, not building systems.
• The line is capacity: stations with an aggregate capacity of 5 MW and up are 691 work.
• Everything below that line — rooftop arrays, commercial building PV, ground-mounts serving a building — stays under Article 690.
• A 691 station is an engineered installation, with its own access, fencing, and documentation rules, and access limited to qualified persons.
• The article was added in the 2017 edition; it is not new in 2020.
Sharma does not build these. The skill this page teaches is recognition: know the article exists, so a plant job is never priced from residential 690 habits.
sections.on_the_job: Recognition only: a plant of 5 MW and up is an engineered, fenced, access-controlled installation with its own documentation rules. If a developer asks Sharma to 'hook up' a solar field outside Ocala, the first move is the capacity math on the plant's one-line: at 5 MW and up, this is a 691 station, and the conversation starts with the plant's engineered drawings — never with residential 690 habits, never with a rooftop takeoff, and never with a price built from 690 material lists.
sections.why_it_exists: A 5 MW plant is a power station, not a big rooftop. Its fault energy, its switching, its access control, and its documentation are engineered the way a utility facility is engineered, and the consequences of treating it like a large residential array land on whoever priced it that way. Article 691 exists so the threshold is unmistakable: cross 5 MW and the job changes articles, changes design method, and changes who may work on it.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating the threshold as a size detail: 'a big array is still Article 690.' At 5 MW aggregate capacity the job leaves 690. Article 691 takes over, and its engineered-design, fencing, access, and documentation rules come with it.
inspection_fails: Plant priced and permitted from a residential 690 takeoff — no engineered design package behind it.
Fencing and controlled access treated as site extras instead of part of the station's installation rules.
Documentation and directories missing at turnover on a plant that requires them.
Unqualified crew working inside the fence — 691 stations are qualified-persons territory.

figures.alt: Scale bar running from a 10 kW house array and building PV under Article 690 to a gold 5 MW line where Article 691 takes over for utility-scale PV stations, with a comparison panel of the two articles covering design basis, fencing, access, and documentation.
figures.caption: 5 MW is the line: 690 below it, 691 at and above it.

page_quiz.question: Article 691 begins at what aggregate PV capacity?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Large-scale PV electric supply stations — 5 MW and up — are Article 691 work; below that, Article 690 governs.

choices: No article — it is utility exempt by size alone
page_quiz.explain_plain: At 6 MW the plant is over the 5 MW line: an engineered 691 station with its own access, fencing, and documentation rules.

sections.title: Article 692 — Fuel Cell Systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 692 covers fuel cell power systems — a chemical generator that makes electricity while fuel reaches it. A system may be stand-alone or interactive with other sources, with or without battery storage (692.1).
• Listing (692.6): the fuel cell system is evaluated and listed for its intended application before it is installed.
• Output sizing (692.8(B)): feeder conductors from the fuel cell to the premises wiring are sized at not less than the greater of the nameplate rated circuit current or the rating of the fuel cell's own overcurrent device.
• Disconnects (692.13, 692.14): a means disconnects all current-carrying conductors of the source from every other conductor in the building; it follows 225.31 and 225.33 through 225.40, and need not be suitable as service equipment.
• Identification (692.4(B)): a permanent plaque or directory at each service location lists the fuel cell with every other power source on site.
• Marking: the power source is marked at its disconnecting means (692.50), the manual fuel shut-off valve's location is marked at the building's primary disconnect (692.51), and a stored-energy warning goes at the service disconnect where the system stores energy (692.52).
• Interactive systems also meet Article 705, and the transfer equipment keeps the fuel cell isolated from the utility network (692.61).
sections.on_the_job: A 10 kW fuel cell on a small commercial job in Orlando: the nameplate rated current is 42 A and the unit's overcurrent device is 50 A, so 692.8(B) sizes the output feeder at the greater number — conductors with at least 50 A ampacity, not the 42 A the nameplate headline suggests. The disconnect beside the unit opens all current-carrying conductors, the service equipment gets a plaque listing the utility service and the fuel cell side by side, and the manual fuel shut-off valve's location is marked at the building's primary disconnect, so a fire crew can find it without a site walk.
sections.why_it_exists: A fuel cell is a generator with no off switch on the machine: while fuel flows, the stack makes power, and stored-energy systems keep terminals live after that. Crews and firefighters trained on 'open the breaker and it is dead' get hurt by quiet backfeed. The disconnect, plaque, and fuel-valve marking rules exist so anyone can find every source on the site, isolate it, and stop the fuel that keeps it alive.
inspection_fails: Output feeder sized to the nameplate current where the fuel cell's overcurrent device was rated higher — 692.8(B) takes the greater.
No plaque or directory at the service equipment identifying the fuel cell as a second power source.
Disconnect opens the ungrounded conductors only; a current-carrying conductor of the source stays connected.
Manual fuel shut-off valve location not marked at the building's primary disconnecting means.
Unlisted fuel cell system set in place — 692.6 requires evaluation and listing for the application before installation.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing the output feeder from the nameplate current alone. 692.8(B) takes the greater of the nameplate rated circuit current and the rating of the fuel cell's overcurrent device — when the unit's device is the bigger number, it governs. And 'disconnect open' is not 'dead': with fuel still flowing, the stack is still a source — which is why the fuel shut-off marking is part of the same job.
