sections.title: Article 694 — Wind Electric Systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 694 covers small wind electric systems: the turbine, its tower, and the generators, alternators, inverters, and controllers that turn wind into premises power, interconnected with the utility or standing alone, with or without battery storage. The article's size line is per turbine — each individual wind turbine must be rated 100 kW or less. Utility-scale machines live under utility rules, not this article.
• The turbine itself is part of the electrical system (694.2 counts the tower, nacelle, and turbine output circuit as system parts), and 694.7 requires the wind electric system to be listed.
• 694.10: on one- and two-family dwellings, the wind turbine output circuit is limited to 600 volts maximum.
• 694.12: system currents are treated as continuous — conductors are sized at not less than 125 percent of the maximum circuit current.
• 694.15: turbine output circuits, inverter output circuits, and storage conductors get overcurrent protection under Article 240, sized on the same 125 percent basis.
• 694.20: a disconnecting means for the system must be readily accessible and open all ungrounded conductors.
• An interactive system interconnects under 694.60 and 694.62, which send you to Article 705, using inverters listed and identified as interactive.
sections.on_the_job: Recognition only: a small wind system's disconnects, grounding, and tower work follow the turbine manufacturer's listing and this article. Sharma's likely piece is the supply-side connection — confirm the turbine's own disconnect and tower grounding are in the turbine installer's scope before pricing ours. If a quote ever does land, the sizing habit to bring is the 125 percent rule: a turbine whose maximum output current is 40 A needs conductors sized for at least 50 A before any temperature or fill adjustment.
sections.why_it_exists: You cannot switch off the wind. A turbine keeps generating as long as the rotor turns, and an unloaded turbine in a gust can overspeed and tear itself apart — so the article builds safety out of listing, continuous-duty sizing, and a real disconnect, instead of pretending the source can be shut down like a utility feed.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing wind circuits like ordinary loads. Wind output is continuous by rule — 694.12 sizes conductors at 125 percent of the maximum circuit current, not the nameplate's fair-weather rating, and the disconnect still has to open every ungrounded conductor.
inspection_fails: Turbine output conductors sized at 100 percent of maximum circuit current instead of 125 percent (694.12).
AC-only breaker protecting a dc turbine output circuit — the device must be rated for the circuit it protects (694.15).
No readily accessible disconnecting means, or one that leaves an ungrounded conductor closed (694.20).
Grid used as the only overspeed protection — an interconnected grid is not an adequate alternate diversion load (694.7).
Unlisted turbine system installed as a field-assembled kit (694.7).

sections.title: Article 695 — Fire Pumps
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 695 exists for one reason: the fire pump must run, even at the cost of the equipment itself. Everything in it runs backward from ordinary motor practice:
• Sources are chosen for reliability above all (695.3).
• Overcurrent devices are sized to carry locked-rotor current indefinitely rather than to trip (695.4).
• Disconnects are arranged so the pump cannot be casually shut off.
Recognition level is the right depth for Sharma: this is engineered, AHJ-scrutinized work, and the pages here cover what to recognize and what never to improvise. The article does not apply to sprinkler-system pumps at one- and two-family dwellings, and pressure-maintenance (jockey) pumps sit outside its scope as pumps — though their current counts in the 695.3 source sizing.
sections.on_the_job: If a bid touches a fire pump, the electrical design comes from the engineer of record and NFPA 20 — Sharma prices the installation of a designed system, never a redesign in the field. On a mid-rise condo job in Orlando, Sharma's scope in the pump room is recognition and installation: dedicated source, listed controller, disconnecting means as drawn. Anything in that room that looks like an ordinary motor circuit is a question for the engineer, not a field fix.

nec2023_change.change: Article 695 now plainly excludes fire suppression water pumps in one- and two-family homes, so a house sprinkler pump isn't treated as a fire pump. New item (4) in 695.1(B) takes fire suppression water pumps in one- and two-family homes out of Article 695.

nec2023_change.change: Diesel-driven fire pumps no longer need a surge-protective device at the controller. Electric fire pumps still do. New exception: a diesel-driven fire pump doesn't need a surge-protective device (SPD) at its controller.

sections.why_it_exists: In a fire, the pump is the water supply for the sprinklers and standpipes. A pump that trips on overload, or that a well-meaning employee switched off last month and forgot, leaves the building defenseless while it burns. Article 695 trades motor protection for run time: burn up the pump if necessary, but keep water moving until the fire is out.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is wiring the fire pump like an Article 430 motor, with overloads sized to trip and save the motor. Under 695.4 the overcurrent device is sized to carry locked-rotor current indefinitely — the pump is expendable, the water supply is not. The second trap is leaving the jockey pump out of the source math: it sits outside the article's scope as a pump, but its current still counts in the 695.3 source sizing.

• 695.1: Article 695 now plainly excludes fire suppression water pumps in one- and two-family homes, so a house sprinkler pump isn't treated as a fire pump. New item (4) in 695.1(B) takes fire suppression water pumps in one- and two-family homes out of Article 695.
• 695.15: Diesel-driven fire pumps no longer need a surge-protective device at the controller. Electric fire pumps still do. New exception: a diesel-driven fire pump doesn't need a surge-protective device (SPD) at its controller.
• 695.6: Every fitting on the controller-to-motor wiring for a fire pump now needs a wet-location listing. The wiring methods and motor connection rules carried over. New 695.6(D)(2): every fitting on the controller-to-motor run has to be listed for wet locations.

sections.title: Power sources — reliable, and sized for locked rotor
sections.plain_explanation:
The fire pump supply must come from a reliable source, and the source is sized for the worst event the pump can produce — a stalled pump drawing locked-rotor current.
• The source must carry the locked-rotor current of the fire pump motor(s), plus the locked-rotor current of the pressure-maintenance (jockey) pump motors, plus 100% of the accessory equipment load. Locked rotor, not full load, is the design event.
• Permitted arrangements include a separate utility service, arranged remote from the normal service so one event cannot take both.
• A tap ahead of the normal service disconnecting means is permitted — but not within the enclosure of that disconnect.
• An on-site standby generator is permitted, protected against fire damage.
• Where transfer equipment is used, it sits in the fire pump room (695.3(F)).
• Phase converters are not permitted as the supply (695.3(I)).
sections.on_the_job: Warehouse job east of Orlando: a 75 hp electric fire pump at 460 V. The motor nameplate shows 96 A full load, but locked rotor works out to roughly 590 A. Add the jockey pump at about 40 A locked rotor and 12 A of accessory load at 100%, and the source has to carry roughly 640 A indefinitely — which is why the fire pump tap lands ahead of the main, and why nobody "right-sizes" that protection down to running current. Recognize the tap-ahead-of-the-main arrangement when you see it on existing work: it is deliberate, not a violation.
sections.figure_idea: One-line: normal service and fire pump tap ahead of the main, generator as second source.
sections.why_it_exists: The pump exists for the worst day in the building's life. If a fire, a fault, or one opened disconnect can kill the normal power and the pump together, the sprinkler system is a decoration. And a seized pump draws locked-rotor current: a source or device that lets go at that current stops the pump at the exact moment the building needs it most.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing the fire pump source the way you size any other motor circuit — from full-load current, with protection that trips on overload. Here the design event is locked rotor: pump locked-rotor plus jockey locked-rotor plus all of the accessory load, carried indefinitely (the protection rule itself is 695.4). An answer built on 96 A running current for a 75 hp pump misses the event the article is written around.

sections.title: Continuity of power — protection that refuses to trip
sections.plain_explanation:
Continuity rules invert ordinary practice. For a fire pump, the design goal is not a circuit that trips — it is a pump that keeps running:
• A single disconnecting means is permitted where it is listed for fire pump service together with the controller (or transfer switch) it feeds
• Its overcurrent device is selected to carry, indefinitely, the sum of the locked-rotor currents of the fire pump and pressure-maintenance motors, plus the full accessory load — and it must be listed for fire pump use
• The disconnect must be lockable in the closed position — the opposite of the elevator rule
• It is identified as a fire pump disconnect with permanently marked letters not less than 1 in. high
• No ground-fault protection of equipment is applied to the fire pump circuit
Anything that can shut the pump down on a fault that is not a short circuit is designed out. The supply behind it is sized the same way — for locked-rotor current, not full load (695.3).
sections.on_the_job: Field recognition: a fire pump disconnect that looks 'oversized' and is locked ON is correct. Never 'fix' one to ordinary motor sizing. On a Lakeland warehouse job, the fire pump disconnect carries a padlock through the closed-position hasp and 1 in. letters reading FIRE PUMP DISCONNECT. If a service call finds one tripping, the answer is to find the fault — not to add GFPE or downsize the device.
sections.figure_idea: Disconnect placard: 'FIRE PUMP DISCONNECT' in 1 in. letters, lock through the closed-position hasp.
sections.why_it_exists: A fire pump that trips on overload during a fire is worse than a pump that burns up running — the building is already on fire, and the pump is the last tool left. Locked-rotor sizing, no GFPE, and a disconnect locked ON all serve one decision made in advance: the pump runs until it cannot, and nothing in the protection scheme is allowed to second-guess that during the event.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answers come from ordinary motor practice: size the device at 125% of full load, add GFPE 'for safety,' or pick a disconnect that locks open. Fire pump rules reverse all three — carry locked-rotor current indefinitely, no ground-fault protection of equipment, and lockable in the closed position.

sections.title: Transformers — dedicated and oversized
sections.plain_explanation:
Transformers that sit between the system supply and the fire pump controller follow this section, not ordinary transformer practice.
• Sizing (695.5(B)): not less than 125% of the fire pump and pressure-maintenance motor loads, plus 100% of the fire-pump accessory equipment the transformer supplies.
• Dedicated, with one door (695.5(C)): only a feeder-source transformer covered by 695.5(C) may also supply loads not directly associated with the fire pump system.
• Protection (695.5(B)): primary overcurrent protection is sized to carry indefinitely the sum of the locked-rotor currents of the fire pump and pressure-maintenance motors, plus the full-load current of the accessory equipment — and no secondary OCPD is permitted. The transformer protection is not allowed to become the weak link that stops the pump.
sections.on_the_job: Warehouse job, 480 V three-phase. Nameplates: fire pump motor 96 A, jockey (pressure-maintenance) motor 11 A, accessory equipment 8 A. Transformer sizing: (96 + 11) × 125% = 134 A, plus 8 A at 100% = 142 A — about 118 kVA, so a 150 kVA unit. The controller submittal lists locked-rotor currents of 578 A and 66 A: the primary device must carry 578 + 66 + 8 = 652 A indefinitely, and there is no secondary breaker to 'correct.' If existing work shows building loads tapped off a fire pump transformer, report it — do not add Sharma loads to it, and do not re-size its protection to ordinary 450.3 sizing.

sections.why_it_exists: In a fire, the pump motor may stall or start against a locked rotor and sit there drawing locked-rotor current. Ordinary protection would trip to save the transformer — and the building loses its water. This section inverts the priority: the transformer is oversized, and its primary device is chosen to carry the locked-rotor sum indefinitely, so electricity is never the reason the pump stops.
inspection_fails: Secondary overcurrent device installed on a fire pump transformer — 695.5(B) does not permit one.
Primary protection sized per 450.3, too small to carry the locked-rotor sum of the pump and jockey motors indefinitely.
Lighting or HVAC panel tapped from a dedicated fire pump transformer that is not a 695.5(C) feeder-source transformer.
Transformer sized at 100% of the motor full-load currents, with the 125% factor of 695.5(B) never applied.
sections.exam_trap: The exam trap is Table 450.3 thinking: size the primary at 125% and add a secondary main for good measure. Both moves fail here — the primary must carry the locked-rotor sum indefinitely, and a secondary OCPD is not permitted at all. The second trap is tapping the 'spare capacity' for a lighting panel: only a 695.5(C) feeder-source transformer may carry other loads.

sections.title: Voltage drop — 15% starting, 5% running
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 695 has one of the few mandatory voltage-drop rules in the NEC — most voltage-drop text elsewhere is only a recommendation. This one is a calculation rule with two limits, and both are checked at the fire pump controller:
• (A) Starting: the voltage at the controller's line terminals must not drop more than 15% below normal (controller-rated) voltage while the motor is starting.
• (B) Running: the voltage at the controller's load terminals must not drop more than 5% below the motor's voltage rating while the motor runs at 115% of its full-load current.
Conductors run under 695.6(B) have to satisfy both tests on top of their ampacity floor. Passing the ampacity table is not enough — on a long pump run, the starting test is usually the one that sizes the wire.
sections.on_the_job: Warehouse job outside Ocala: the fire pump room sits about 350 ft from the service, so the feeder is long. The controller is rated 480 V, so the starting floor is 85% — 408 V at the controller's line terminals during the start. The motor is rated 460 V, so running at 115% of full-load current the load terminals must hold at least 95% — 437 V. The crew sizes the run for ampacity first, then runs the starting check; on this length the starting check wins and the conductors go up a size. Nobody on the job 'fixes' a failed check by swapping in a bigger breaker — the fix is copper.
sections.figure_idea: Voltage profile along a long pump feeder: 15% dip envelope at start, 5% at run.

nec2023_change.change: Fire pump voltage drop was rebuilt around the fire pump installation standard's limits: 15 percent starting, 5 percent running, with two starting carve-outs that need a proven generator start. Starting (695.7(A)): the controller's line terminals must hold at least 85 percent of the controller's rated voltage.

sections.why_it_exists: A fire pump that cannot start is a sprinkler system with no water behind it. Locked-rotor inrush drags the voltage down hard; if the dip is too deep the motor stalls or the controller drops out, and the pump never comes up to pressure while the building burns. The running limit protects the motor itself: a motor held at low voltage under load overheats and can fail mid-fire.
inspection_fails: Feeder sized from the ampacity table only; no starting voltage-drop calculation for a long pump run.
Running drop checked at nameplate full-load current instead of 115% of full-load current.
Voltage drop measured (or calculated) at the service instead of at the controller terminals.
Conductors meet the 695.6(B) ampacity floor but the starting dip pulls the controller below 85% of its rating.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is reaching for the familiar numbers from 210.19 and 215.2 — 3% on a branch circuit, 5% total. Those are informational-note recommendations for ordinary work, not the fire pump rule, and they measure the wrong event. On a 695.7 question the pair is 15% starting and 5% running, checked at the controller, with the running check made at 115% of full-load current — not at nameplate full load.
